messages.content: Our customers table uses email as the primary key and orders reference it. Marketing now wants people to be able to change their email. What breaks, and what should the key have been?
Watch what a routine email change does when the email is also the join target. First the design as it stands, with foreign keys enforced:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_email TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(email), total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES ('ana@old.com', 'Ana Ruiz'), ('bo@old.com', 'Bo Lind')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'ana@old.com', 4200), (2, 'ana@old.com', 1850), (3, 'bo@old.com', 990)
UPDATE customers SET email = 'ana@new.com' WHERE email = 'ana@old.com'

messages.content: The update fails outright: orders 1 and 2 point at 'ana@old.com', and with no ON UPDATE CASCADE the foreign key blocks the rename. Even with CASCADE declared, you would be rewriting every referencing row for what is really an attribute change, and any external system that stored the email as its link (invoices, exports, support tickets) is silently orphaned. The design error is making a mutable, user-controlled attribute load-bearing. Email is a fine UNIQUE business key - it identifies the customer for login and dedupe - but the primary key should have been an immutable surrogate id assigned at insert and never shown a reason to change. Rule of thumb: a primary key's only job is identity inside the database; the moment a value has a life outside (people retype it, change it, merge it), it belongs in a UNIQUE column, not in every foreign key in the schema.
For order_lines, a colleague wants a single auto-increment id as the primary key and says a composite key is old-fashioned. The table holds order_id, line_no, sku, qty. Who is right?
The composite key is not nostalgia here - it states a real invariant. Watch it work, then note what the surrogate-only version would let through:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE order_lines (order_id INTEGER NOT NULL, line_no INTEGER NOT NULL, sku TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no))
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (501, 1, 'MUG-RED', 2), (501, 2, 'TEA-GRN', 1), (502, 1, 'MUG-RED', 1)
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (501, 2, 'POT-HND', 1)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: order_lines.order_id, order_lines.line_no

arguments.sql: SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS lines, SUM(qty) AS units FROM order_lines GROUP BY order_id ORDER BY order_id

messages.content: The fourth insert is rejected: order 501 already has a line 2, and 'an order cannot list the same line number twice' is exactly the kind of rule a primary key should enforce for free. A lone auto-increment id would have accepted it, pushing the check into application code where one missed code path corrupts data. The composite key also matches how the table is actually read - all lines of an order, in line order - so the key doubles as the natural clustering and sort. A surrogate id earns its place when other tables need to reference one specific line (a returns table pointing at a single line, say). Then keep both: surrogate id as primary key for referencing, plus UNIQUE(order_id, line_no) so the invariant survives. What you should not do is add the id and drop the composite uniqueness - that is how 'old-fashioned' turns into duplicate line 2s.
We are picking primary keys for a table that will hold about 200 million rows: integer, UUID, or the UUID stored as text. Can you price the difference before we argue about it?
The key is copied into every index on the table, so width is not an aesthetic choice. Pricing the raw payload first (indexes carry per-entry overhead too, but width is the part we control):

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE keytest (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT)
INSERT INTO keytest VALUES (1, 'int key is the rowid itself')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows FROM keytest

messages.content: Payload alone: 1.6 GB for 8-byte integers, 3.2 GB for 16-byte binary UUIDs, 7.2 GB for UUIDs stored as 36-character text - and that is per index that carries the key, before page overhead. Integers win on size and on insert locality: sequential values append at the right edge of the B-tree, while random UUIDs scatter inserts across pages and fragment the index over time. UUIDs earn their keep when ids are minted in many places without coordination (offline devices, merged databases, ids exposed in URLs that must not be enumerable or leak row counts). The middle path most systems land on: integer surrogate inside the database, plus a separate public_id UUID column with a unique index for anything the outside world sees. And if you do store UUIDs, store the 16 bytes, never the 36-character string - the text form costs more than double for zero extra information.
Students enroll in courses - classic many-to-many. Should the enrollments table get its own id column, or is (student_id, course_id) enough?
Start with the pair as the key and see which bad states it makes impossible:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER NOT NULL, course_id INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id))
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (7, 101), (7, 102), (9, 101), (11, 103)
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (7, 101)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: enrollments.student_id, enrollments.course_id

arguments.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS students FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id ORDER BY course_id

messages.content: The duplicate (7, 101) insert is rejected by the key itself: a student cannot enroll in the same course twice, and no application code had to remember to check. For a pure junction - a table whose entire meaning is 'this pair exists' - the composite primary key is the design; an extra id adds a second way to identify the same fact and invites other tables to reference a pairing as if it were a thing. Add a surrogate id only when the pairing becomes a thing in its own right: when enrollments gain a lifecycle other tables point at (payments for this enrollment, a grade appeal against this enrollment), or when the pair stops being unique (a student retakes the course next term, so term joins the key or an id takes over). Until then, (student_id, course_id) is not a shortcut - it is the constraint that keeps the data honest.
A signup form dedupes people by UNIQUE(name, phone). It just rejected a real second customer. What went wrong with the key choice?
The constraint assumed a fact about the world that is not true. Here is the rejection happening to two different people:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE people (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, phone TEXT NOT NULL, UNIQUE (name, phone))
INSERT INTO people VALUES (1, 'Sam Lee', '555-0142')
INSERT INTO people VALUES (2, 'Sam Lee', '555-0142')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: people.name, people.phone

Both rows describe a Sam Lee reachable at 555-0142 - and they are genuinely two people: a father and son sharing a name and a household landline, roommates on one mobile plan, a junior who inherited a recycled number. The insert fails because UNIQUE(name, phone) encodes the claim 'name plus phone identifies a person', which was never verified - it was just plausible. This is the mirror image of a missing constraint: an over-strong uniqueness rule corrupts too, by refusing reality. Before making any column set unique, ask what evidence would prove two rows with the same values must be the same entity. Email plus a verified-account flag might carry that weight; name and phone do not. The repair: keep a surrogate id, drop the composite uniqueness to a non-unique index for lookup speed, and let dedupe be a reviewable merge workflow over candidates, not a hard wall at insert time.
Our events table keys rows by (account_id, created_at timestamp). A report that replays events in order occasionally processes two events swapped. Why, and what key fixes it?
Timestamps are not a sequence - two events in the same tick are tied, and ties have no order. Demonstrating with two events written in the same millisecond:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE events (account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, created_at TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (account_id, created_at))
INSERT INTO events VALUES (8, '2026-05-01T10:00:00.000', 'debit')
INSERT INTO events VALUES (8, '2026-05-01T10:00:00.000', 'credit')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: events.account_id, events.created_at

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS stored FROM events

messages.content: The second same-millisecond insert does not even survive: the primary key treats it as a duplicate and rejects it, so the design first loses events, and if the key is dropped to stop the losses, replay order between tied events becomes whatever the storage engine feels like - hence swapped debits and credits. The fix is to key events by something that is actually sequential: (account_id, seq), where seq is a per-account counter allocated at write time (1, 2, 3, ... per account). The pair stays unique, replays sort deterministically by seq, and the timestamp remains as an ordinary attribute for display and range scans. The general lesson: never let a measurement of when stand in for an ordering. Clocks tick coarsely, skew between machines, and repeat; a counter allocated by the single writer who owns the sequence cannot tie. If several writers append concurrently, allocate seq from one sequence object or a single-writer log - the key design and the write protocol have to be chosen together.
Sensor readings land in readings(sensor_id, ts, value) with PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, ts). A sensor that reports twice in the same second gets rejected. Is the key wrong?
The key is doing exactly what it was told - the real question is what a duplicate (sensor, second) means in this domain:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE readings (sensor_id INTEGER NOT NULL, ts TEXT NOT NULL, value REAL NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, ts))
INSERT INTO readings VALUES (4, '2026-05-01 10:00:01', 21.6)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: readings.sensor_id, readings.ts

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS readings_kept FROM readings

messages.content: Three readings are kept and the fourth - sensor 4 reporting 21.6 in a second where it already reported 21.4 - is rejected. Whether that is a bug depends on the instrument: if the sensor samples once per second, a second value in the same second is a retransmission or a clock glitch, and rejecting it is the key protecting you. If the sensor can genuinely sample faster than the timestamp's resolution, the key is lying about identity: the readings differ, so (sensor_id, ts) is not a key at all, it is a rounding. The repairs, in order of preference: raise timestamp resolution if the device has it (milliseconds make collisions honest rarities); add a device-supplied reading counter to the key, (sensor_id, device_seq), which is the sensor-world version of a sequence number; or, last resort, add an arrival id and accept that dedupe becomes a query, not a constraint. What not to do: drop the primary key to make the error go away - you would trade a loud rejection for silent double-counted averages.
If we give users a surrogate id as primary key, do we still need anything on email? A test just created two accounts with the same email.
A surrogate key identifies rows; it says nothing about which real-world facts must stay unique. Here is the gap, and the standard two-key pattern closing it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'kim@x.com', 'Kim A')
INSERT INTO users VALUES (2, 'kim@x.com', 'Kim B')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS accounts FROM users

messages.content: The second insert is rejected - not by the primary key (id 2 was free) but by the UNIQUE constraint on email. This pairing is the default shape for most entity tables: a surrogate primary key that never changes and exists only for joins, plus one unique constraint per real-world identifier the business cannot afford to duplicate (email here; maybe a national id or an account number elsewhere). Skipping the unique constraints because 'we have an id now' is how duplicate accounts are born: the id guarantees rows are distinct, not that people are. When you design a table, list the two sets separately - what identifies a row to the database (primary key), and what identifies the entity to the world (unique business keys) - and make sure both lists are enforced. The test that created two accounts was not a test bug; it was the schema telling you the second list was empty.

A legacy table has no id: warehouses are identified by a code like 'WH-04', and stock rows reference that code. It works, but a senior dev says foreign keys should always point at an integer id. Should we refactor?
Foreign keys may reference any unique column, not only a surrogate id. The legacy design, working as intended:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE warehouses (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE stock (warehouse_code TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES warehouses(code), sku TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (warehouse_code, sku))
INSERT INTO warehouses VALUES ('WH-04', 'Reno'), ('WH-09', 'Tulsa')
INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('WH-04', 'BOLT-M6', 340), ('WH-09', 'BOLT-M6', 125)
SELECT warehouse_code, qty FROM stock WHERE sku = 'BOLT-M6' ORDER BY warehouse_code

messages.content: It works, and it is defensible: the warehouse code is short, human-meaningful in every log line and report, assigned by the business, and - the crucial test - it never changes and is never reused. A foreign key needs a stable unique target, not a particular data type. Refactoring to integer ids would buy narrower joins and cost a mapping every human reader now does for free. The refactor becomes worth it the day any of the code's virtues fail: if codes get reissued after a warehouse closes, if two merged companies arrive with colliding code schemes, or if codes start encoding mutable facts (a city prefix in a code whose warehouse relocates). Judge a natural key by its lifecycle, not its type. 'Always reference an integer id' is a good default for new tables with invented identifiers; it is not a law that justifies churning a stable, meaningful code that the whole company already reads fluently.
Design the keys for an address book: people can have several addresses (home, work, cabin), and other tables need to point at one specific address. What goes where?
Two different identification jobs again - finding a person's addresses, and pinning one exact address from elsewhere:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE people (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE addresses (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, person_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES people(id), kind TEXT NOT NULL, street TEXT NOT NULL, UNIQUE (person_id, kind))
INSERT INTO people VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lind')
INSERT INTO addresses VALUES (10, 1, 'home', '12 Oak St'), (11, 1, 'work', '400 Pine Ave'), (12, 2, 'home', '9 Elm Rd')
INSERT INTO addresses VALUES (13, 1, 'home', '77 Duplicate Ln')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: addresses.person_id, addresses.kind

arguments.sql: SELECT person_id, COUNT(*) AS addresses FROM addresses GROUP BY person_id ORDER BY person_id

messages.content: Addresses get their own surrogate id as primary key, because shipments and invoices need to reference one specific address and keep referencing it even if its text is later corrected. The person link is a plain foreign key, and the business rule 'one home address per person' (if that is the rule) rides on UNIQUE(person_id, kind) - which is what just rejected the second 'home' row for Ana while happily allowing her work address. Note what did not get a key: the street text. Two people can share an address and one person can fix a typo, so street is data, not identity. If deliveries later need 'the address as it was on the day we shipped', that is not a key problem at all - it is a snapshot: copy the address text onto the shipment row at ship time, because the shipment's truth is historical, not a live join.
Logins keep colliding: 'Ana@X.com' registered last year, and today 'ana@x.com' created a second account. The email column has a UNIQUE constraint. Why didn't it fire?
Because text uniqueness in most databases is case-sensitive byte comparison, and email local parts are not. Demonstrating the hole, then the one-word fix:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE logins (email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, created TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO logins VALUES ('Ana@X.com', '2025-11-02')
INSERT INTO logins VALUES ('ana@x.com', '2026-05-01')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS accounts FROM logins

messages.content: Both inserts succeed: to a binary-collated UNIQUE constraint, 'Ana@X.com' and 'ana@x.com' are simply different strings, so the schema kept a promise the business never meant - byte uniqueness - while the business needed case-insensitive identity. The repairs: declare the column UNIQUE with COLLATE NOCASE (in engines that support per-column collation), store a normalized form (lowercased, trimmed) in its own column and put the uniqueness there, or normalize on write and keep the display form separately. The normalized-column pattern is the most portable and the most honest: email_display preserves what the user typed, email_key is what identity means. The broader lesson generalizes to usernames, SKUs, and coupon codes: whenever humans type an identifier, ask 'what variations count as the same?' - case, surrounding spaces, accents, leading zeros - and encode that answer in a canonical form the constraint can actually compare.

Our inventory table will be queried two ways: 'all stock for a store' and 'which stores carry this SKU'. Does the primary key order (store_id, sku) versus (sku, store_id) actually matter? Give me the comparison.

Yes - a composite key (and its backing index) serves prefix lookups, so column order decides which query is native and which needs help.

| Query | PK (store_id, sku) | PK (sku, store_id) |
|---|---|---|
| All stock for one store | Direct prefix scan, rows already grouped by store | Full scan or a second index |
| Which stores carry a SKU | Full scan or a second index | Direct prefix scan, rows grouped by SKU |
| One exact (store, SKU) row | Fast | Fast |
| All SKUs, sorted, across stores | Scan + sort | Scan in key order |

The rule: put first the column your dominant query filters by equality and wants grouped. If both queries are truly hot, no single ordering wins - keep the primary key on the pair that matches the table's identity reads and add a plain index on the reversed pair; the extra index costs write time and storage, which is the honest price of serving both access paths. What order does not affect: correctness of uniqueness - (store_id, sku) and (sku, store_id) reject exactly the same duplicates.
When is a natural key actually the right choice for a primary key? I keep hearing 'always surrogate' but country and currency tables feel different.

Country and currency tables feel different because they are different: their keys pass tests that invented identifiers fail. A natural key is a sound primary key when the value is (1) assigned by an authority outside your system, so you will never need to invent or reissue it - ISO country and currency codes qualify; (2) genuinely immutable - FR will not stop meaning France, and if a code is ever retired it is retired forever, not recycled onto a different country; (3) short and stable in format, so joins and storage stay cheap; and (4) meaningful to readers, so a row that says currency='JPY' explains itself in every report without a join. Reference and lookup data maintained by standards bodies is the natural home of natural keys. The 'always surrogate' heuristic exists because most entity identifiers - emails, usernames, SKUs, phone numbers - fail at least one test: they change, get recycled, collide across mergers, or encode facts that stop being true. So the rule is not surrogate versus natural; it is: use a natural key when its lifecycle is governed by someone more reliable than your application, and a surrogate whenever your own system is the authority that might change its mind.
Our orders table stores customer_name on every order row. A customer just rebranded and now appears under two names in the same report. Show me the failure and the redesign.
This is the textbook update anomaly, executed. Phase one: the denormalized table, a rename applied to only some rows (one code path missed the rest):

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders_flat (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, customer_name TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders_flat VALUES (1, 7, 'Ana Ruiz Studio', 4200), (2, 7, 'Ana Ruiz Studio', 1850), (3, 7, 'Ana Ruiz Studio', 2600), (4, 8, 'Bo Lind', 990)
UPDATE orders_flat SET customer_name = 'Ruiz Atelier' WHERE id IN (1, 2)
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(DISTINCT customer_name) AS names_on_file FROM orders_flat GROUP BY customer_id

messages.content: Customer 7 now has two distinct names on file, and both are 'true' as far as the database knows - reports group by name and split her history in half. Nothing malfunctioned; the schema stored one fact (a customer's name) in thousands of places and a partial update is inevitable at scale. The redesign stores the fact once: customers(id, name) and orders(id, customer_id, total_cents), with the rename touching exactly one row and every report joining to the single current truth. Note the deliberate exception this does not cover: the name printed on an issued invoice is history, not current truth - that one belongs as a snapshot copy on the invoice itself. Normalization is not 'never copy'; it is 'know which copy is the living fact and which is a fossil, and only let the living one be joined to.'
Course planning wants to list a new course, 'Ceramics 101', before anyone enrolls. Our only table is enrollments(student, course_title, room). They say it can't be done. Are they right?
They are - this is the insert anomaly. A course with no students has no row to live in:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_flat (student TEXT NOT NULL, course_title TEXT NOT NULL, room TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (student, course_title))
INSERT INTO enrollments_flat VALUES ('Mina', 'Ceramics 100', 'Studio B'), ('Theo', 'Ceramics 100', 'Studio B')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_needed_for_empty_course FROM enrollments_flat WHERE course_title = 'Ceramics 101'

messages.content: Zero rows, and there is no honest row to insert: the primary key demands a student, so 'Ceramics 101 exists, meets in Studio B, currently has nobody in it' is unrepresentable without enrolling a fake person. The table fused two entities - courses and enrollments - into one, so each inherited the other's existence rules. Split them: courses(course_id, title, room) holds Ceramics 101 happily on its own; enrollments(student_id, course_id) records only real pairings. The diagnostic to carry away: whenever 'we cannot put X in the system until Y happens' sounds wrong, check whether X and Y were glued into one table. Insert anomalies are existence rules leaking across entities, and the cure is always the same - give each entity its own table so it can exist at its own pace.
When the last student dropped 'Ceramics 100', the course vanished from our catalog entirely - room assignment, everything. The data was in the enrollments table. What happened?
The delete anomaly: the last enrollment row was carrying facts that were never the enrollment's to carry.

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments_flat (student TEXT NOT NULL, course_title TEXT NOT NULL, room TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (student, course_title))
INSERT INTO enrollments_flat VALUES ('Mina', 'Ceramics 100', 'Studio B')
DELETE FROM enrollments_flat WHERE student = 'Mina' AND course_title = 'Ceramics 100'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS course_facts_left FROM enrollments_flat WHERE course_title = 'Ceramics 100'

messages.content: Deleting Mina's enrollment deleted the course: its title and room existed only as passengers on enrollment rows, so the last drop took the catalog entry with it. The schema could not distinguish 'this pairing ended' from 'this course ceased to exist' because it stored both facts in the same rows. After the split into courses and enrollments, the same drop removes one enrollment row and the course row - title, room, capacity - sits untouched, ready to be offered again next term. Delete anomalies are the quietest of the three classic anomalies because nothing errors; information just evaporates as a side effect of an unrelated operation. Audit for them by asking of every table: 'if I delete the last row mentioning X, what else do I lose?' If the answer names a different entity, that entity needs its own table.
A reviewer flagged our invoice_lines for storing unit_price_cents when products already has a price column - 'redundant, normalize it'. Should we remove it?
No - and removing it would corrupt history. Watch what the products price does over time versus what an issued invoice must keep saying:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE invoice_lines (invoice_id INTEGER NOT NULL, sku TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO products VALUES ('MUG-RED', 1200)
INSERT INTO invoice_lines VALUES (9001, 'MUG-RED', 2, 1200)
UPDATE products SET price_cents = 1500 WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'
SELECT qty * unit_price_cents AS invoice_line_total FROM invoice_lines WHERE invoice_id = 9001

messages.content: The product now costs 1500, and invoice 9001 still totals 2400 - correctly, because the customer was charged 1200 on the day. unit_price_cents on the line is not a copy of the product's price; it is a different fact that merely had the same value at the moment of sale: the price agreed in this transaction. Joining to products at report time would retroactively reprice every historical invoice each time the catalog changes - the one outcome accounting cannot tolerate. This is the principled exception to 'store each fact once': facts about events are snapshots of the world at event time. Prices on invoices, addresses on shipments, tax rates on orders, names on certificates - all are fossils by design. The reviewer's instinct is right for living facts (the catalog price lives in exactly one place); it misfires when the copied value's meaning is 'what was true then', because then it was never the same fact at all.
Post pages were slow because every render ran COUNT(*) over comments. We added a comment_count column on posts maintained by triggers. How do we know the triggers keep it true?
A cached counter is a promise the write path must keep. Here is the mechanism doing its job on inserts and deletes:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE posts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT NOT NULL, comment_count INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)
CREATE TABLE comments (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, post_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES posts(id), body TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TRIGGER trg_comment_add AFTER INSERT ON comments BEGIN UPDATE posts SET comment_count = comment_count + 1 WHERE id = NEW.post_id; END
CREATE TRIGGER trg_comment_del AFTER DELETE ON comments BEGIN UPDATE posts SET comment_count = comment_count - 1 WHERE id = OLD.post_id; END
INSERT INTO posts VALUES (1, 'Launch notes', 0)
INSERT INTO comments VALUES (1, 1, 'First!'), (2, 1, 'Congrats'), (3, 1, 'Question...')
DELETE FROM comments WHERE id = 2
SELECT comment_count FROM posts WHERE id = 1
SELECT COUNT(*) AS ground_truth FROM comments WHERE post_id = 1

messages.content: Trigger count and ground truth agree at 2 after three inserts and a delete. That agreement is the design's ongoing obligation, not a one-time property: the counter is denormalized derived data, and every path that changes comments must maintain it - the triggers cover inserts and deletes, but a bulk import that bypasses them, a manual fix-up, or a future 'move comment to another post' feature (an UPDATE of post_id, which neither trigger handles) will drift it silently. Two practices make cached aggregates safe rather than hopeful: first, prefer triggers or a single write service over application code scattered across endpoints, so the maintenance lives at the data layer; second, run a periodic reconciliation - exactly the comparison above, counter versus COUNT(*) - and alert on drift instead of discovering it in a user report. Denormalization is a loan against write-path discipline; reconciliation is how you know the payments are being made.

Our accounts table stores balance_cents, and transactions also exist. Finance found an account where they disagree by 2500 cents. How does a schema let this happen, and how do we find every drifted account?
Two writable copies of one fact will eventually disagree - the only question is whether you can enumerate the damage. The reconciliation is one query:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, balance_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE txns (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, account_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id), amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 10000), (2, 5000), (3, 7250)
UPDATE accounts SET balance_cents = 7250 WHERE id = 3

SELECT a.id, a.balance_cents, COALESCE(SUM(t.amount_cents), 0) AS ledger_sum, a.balance_cents - COALESCE(SUM(t.amount_cents), 0) AS drift FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN txns t ON t.account_id = a.id GROUP BY a.id HAVING drift != 0

messages.content: Account 3 is the only drifter: stored 7250 against a ledger sum of 4750, drift exactly 2500 - someone (a refund script, a manual correction, a bug) wrote the balance without writing the transaction, and the schema had no opinion about it. The deep fix is to demote one of the two to derived status. Cleanest: balance is not stored at all; it is SUM(amount) over an append-only ledger, and the transactions table becomes the single source of truth that can be audited entry by entry. If read performance genuinely needs a stored balance, then it is a cache with rules: only one code path may write it, always in the same transaction as the ledger insert, and the reconciliation query above runs on a schedule with drift treated as an incident, not a curiosity. What you cannot do is keep two independently writable copies and hope - hope is not a consistency mechanism, and finance will always find the 2500 cents before you do.
Posts store tags as one text column like 'ceramics,art,glaze'. Search for tag 'art' also returns posts tagged only 'artist' and 'start'. Is a join table really necessary for something this small?
The substring false positive, executed - then the same question against a junction table:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE posts_csv (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tags TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO posts_csv VALUES (1, 'ceramics,art,glaze'), (2, 'artist,studio'), (3, 'start,process')
SELECT id FROM posts_csv WHERE tags LIKE '%art%' ORDER BY id
CREATE TABLE post_tags (post_id INTEGER NOT NULL, tag TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (post_id, tag))
INSERT INTO post_tags VALUES (1, 'ceramics'), (1, 'art'), (1, 'glaze'), (2, 'artist'), (2, 'studio'), (3, 'start'), (3, 'process')
SELECT post_id FROM post_tags WHERE tag = 'art'

messages.content: The LIKE search returns all three posts; only post 1 is actually tagged 'art' - 'artist' and 'start' are substring accidents, and no amount of delimiter cleverness fully fixes it (a tag containing the delimiter, a tag that is a prefix of another, case variants). The junction table answers with an equality lookup: exactly post 1. But correctness is only half the indictment. In the CSV design you also cannot rename a tag in one place, cannot count posts per tag without string surgery, cannot enforce that tags come from an approved vocabulary, and cannot index tag membership properly. Comma-joined lists are a first-normal-form violation that feels free at insert time and bills you on every read forever. The junction table is three columns and one primary key; for anything queried by membership - tags, categories, permissions, ingredients - it is not over-engineering, it is the data model telling the truth about a many-to-many fact.
Contacts have columns phone1, phone2, phone3. Finding 'who owns number X' takes a three-way OR and we still miss people with four numbers. What's the modeling fix?
Repeating groups: the same fact smeared across columns. The query pain first, then the child-table shape that ends it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE contacts_flat (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, phone1 TEXT, phone2 TEXT, phone3 TEXT)
INSERT INTO contacts_flat VALUES (1, 'Ana', '555-01', '555-02', NULL), (2, 'Bo', NULL, '555-03', NULL)
SELECT id FROM contacts_flat WHERE phone1 = '555-03' OR phone2 = '555-03' OR phone3 = '555-03'
CREATE TABLE phones (contact_id INTEGER NOT NULL, phone TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (contact_id, phone))
INSERT INTO phones VALUES (1, '555-01', 'mobile'), (1, '555-02', 'work'), (2, '555-03', 'mobile')
SELECT contact_id FROM phones WHERE phone = '555-03'

messages.content: Both queries find Bo, but look at their shapes: the flat one names every column and silently fails the day a phone4 appears (and someone always has a fourth number), while the child-table one is a single equality that works for a contact with one phone or nine. Repeating groups break the basic contract of a column - 'values in this column are comparable and searchable as a set' - because the set is spread sideways. Moving phones to a child table also buys what columns never can: a kind per number (mobile, work), a primary flag, an added-on date, and a uniqueness rule like 'a number belongs to one contact' enforced across all numbers at once. The pattern to recognize is any column with a number in its name: phone1..3, address_line2 is fine (it is a different fact), but numbered copies of the same fact are a table trying to be born. Let it - child tables are cheap, and OR-chains over numbered columns are forever.
order_lines stores line_total_cents next to qty and unit_price_cents. A quantity edit just left the total stale. How do we make the derived value impossible to desync?
A stored derived column is a cache with no maintainer. The desync first, then the generated column that removes the write path entirely:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE lines_bad (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, line_total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO lines_bad VALUES (1, 2, 1200, 2400)
UPDATE lines_bad SET qty = 3 WHERE id = 1
SELECT qty, unit_price_cents, line_total_cents, qty * unit_price_cents AS true_total FROM lines_bad WHERE id = 1
CREATE TABLE lines_good (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, line_total_cents INTEGER GENERATED ALWAYS AS (qty * unit_price_cents) STORED)
INSERT INTO lines_good (id, qty, unit_price_cents) VALUES (1, 2, 1200)
UPDATE lines_good SET qty = 3 WHERE id = 1
SELECT qty, line_total_cents FROM lines_good WHERE id = 1

messages.content: In the bad table the row now claims qty 3 at 1200 with a total of 2400 - arithmetic the database watched happen and said nothing about, because line_total_cents was just another writable column. In the good table the same update yields 3600 automatically: a GENERATED ALWAYS column has no write path, so there is nothing to forget. The decision ladder for any derived value: compute it in the query if reads are cheap and rare; expose it as a generated column (or a view) when it must appear in results and stay provably in sync; store and maintain it only when computation is genuinely expensive at read time, and then treat it as a cache with an owner and a reconciliation. The anti-pattern is the middle state most schemas drift into - stored, writable, and maintained by the good intentions of every future editor of the code.
We keep a daily_sales summary table refreshed from orders every night for the dashboard. The owner asked why Tuesday's numbers changed on Wednesday. Is the summary table a mistake?
Not a mistake - a snapshot with a refresh contract. The mechanics, and where the confusion actually comes from:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, day TEXT NOT NULL, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders_count INTEGER NOT NULL, revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO daily_sales SELECT day, COUNT(*), SUM(total_cents) FROM orders GROUP BY day
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (4, '2026-05-05', 700)
SELECT day, revenue_cents FROM daily_sales ORDER BY day
DELETE FROM daily_sales
INSERT INTO daily_sales SELECT day, COUNT(*), SUM(total_cents) FROM orders GROUP BY day
SELECT day, revenue_cents FROM daily_sales ORDER BY day

messages.content: Before the refresh, Tuesday (2026-05-05) reads 6050; after it, 6750 - the late-arriving order 4 was always real, the summary was just stale. Tuesday's numbers 'changed' because the summary is a photograph, not a window: it answers 'what did we know at refresh time', and any late or corrected source row rewrites the photo on the next refresh. That is a legitimate, often necessary design - dashboards should not re-aggregate millions of orders per view - provided three things are explicit: the refresh cadence is displayed with the data ('as of 06:00'), late-arriving facts are expected and their effect understood, and the source of truth remains the orders table, from which the summary can always be rebuilt from scratch, as the delete-and-rebuild above shows. A summary you cannot regenerate is not a summary; it is a second, worse ledger. Keep the rebuild path tested and the staleness labeled, and the owner's question answers itself.
Shipments store zip, city, state on every row. We found zip 60614 paired with two different cities. Which dependency is the schema failing to model?
City and state are facts about the zip, not about the shipment - and storing them per-shipment lets them contradict each other:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE shipments_flat (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, zip TEXT NOT NULL, city TEXT NOT NULL, state TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO shipments_flat VALUES (1, '60614', 'Chicago', 'IL'), (2, '60614', 'Chicago', 'IL'), (3, '60614', 'Chicagoo', 'IL'), (4, '90210', 'Beverly Hills', 'CA')
SELECT zip, COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS city_variants FROM shipments_flat GROUP BY zip HAVING city_variants > 1
CREATE TABLE zips (zip TEXT PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT NOT NULL, state TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO zips VALUES ('60614', 'Chicago', 'IL'), ('90210', 'Beverly Hills', 'CA')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS zip_rows FROM zips

messages.content: Zip 60614 shows two city variants - one is a typo, but the schema cannot tell you which, because it stored the zip-to-city fact once per shipment and the copies drifted. The dependency is zip -> (city, state): a functional dependency whose left side is not the table's key, which is precisely what third normal form forbids. Moving it to a zips table stores the fact once; shipments keep only the zip, and a typo becomes impossible rather than merely unlikely - there is a single row to get right. Two honest caveats: first, real zip data has edge cases (zips spanning city boundaries, preferred versus acceptable city names), so treat the zips table as curated reference data, possibly licensed, not something to hand-maintain from memory. Second, the address as shipped to is again a snapshot - the shipment keeps the full address text it used, while the zips table governs validation and defaults. Normalization decides where a fact is maintained; snapshots decide what an event remembers.
The catalog team wants to copy category_name onto every product row 'for read speed'. Category renames happen a few times a year. Price both designs honestly before we decide.
The cost of a copied fact is paid on the write side, in rows touched per rename. Counting the touch in miniature, then scaling it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products_flat (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, category_name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO products_flat VALUES ('A1', 'Mugs'), ('A2', 'Mugs'), ('A3', 'Mugs'), ('A4', 'Mugs'), ('B1', 'Teas')
UPDATE products_flat SET category_name = 'Stoneware Mugs' WHERE category_name = 'Mugs'

messages.content: In miniature, the rename touched 4 rows where a normalized categories table would touch 1. Scaled to a 2,000,000-product catalog where the renamed category covers 40% of rows, one rename becomes an 800,000-row update - with its locks, WAL churn, replication lag, and the window where readers see both names - versus a single-row update in the normalized design. That is the price, and sometimes it is worth paying: if product reads outnumber renames by millions to one and the join measurably hurts, copy the name, but copy it as a managed cache - written by one code path, rebuilt or reconciled on a schedule, with the categories table still the source of truth. What the pricing exercise prevents is the accidental version: copying for a speculative read win, then discovering the write cost during a rebrand at 2 a.m. Denormalization decisions should always name both numbers - reads saved per day, rows touched per change - before anyone says yes.
Give me a decision rule for when to denormalize that I can apply in design reviews without a two-hour debate.

Use this sequence, in order, and stop at the first step that resolves it. (1) Normalize first, always: the burden of proof is on the copy, because the normalized schema is the only one that cannot contradict itself. (2) Denormalize only against a measured read problem - a profiled query, a named dashboard, a latency budget being missed - never against a hypothetical one; 'might be slow someday' buys complexity today for a benefit that may never arrive. (3) Classify the copy before building it: snapshot of an event (price on an invoice) is not denormalization at all, keep it without guilt; derived data (counters, sums, search text) is a cache and needs an owner, a single maintenance path, and a reconciliation job; duplicated living facts (names, statuses copied between tables) are the dangerous kind and need the strongest justification. (4) Write the price in the design doc: rows touched per update, staleness window, rebuild procedure. If nobody can state the price, the answer is no. (5) Whatever you copy, the normalized original stays the source of truth and the copy must be regenerable from it. Applied consistently, this rule approves the copies that pay (hot counters, reporting summaries) and blocks the ones that merely feel convenient - which is exactly the split a design review exists to make.
A timetable table has (course, teacher, room): each course has one teacher, and each teacher always uses the same room. A teacher's room change updated some rows and not others. Untangle this.
Two dependencies live in this table: course -> teacher and teacher -> room. The second one is the troublemaker, because room is stored once per course:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE timetable_flat (course TEXT PRIMARY KEY, teacher TEXT NOT NULL, room TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO timetable_flat VALUES ('Ceramics 100', 'Mina', 'Studio B'), ('Ceramics 200', 'Mina', 'Studio B'), ('Glazing 101', 'Theo', 'Lab 2')
UPDATE timetable_flat SET room = 'Studio C' WHERE course = 'Ceramics 100'
SELECT teacher, COUNT(DISTINCT room) AS rooms FROM timetable_flat GROUP BY teacher HAVING rooms > 1

messages.content: Mina now teaches in two rooms at once, according to the data - because 'Mina's room' was stored on every course row and the update reached one of them. This is the same shape as the zip/city problem one level deeper (a Boyce-Codd violation): teacher -> room is a dependency on a non-key attribute, so room is repeated wherever the teacher appears. Split by dependency: courses(course, teacher) and teachers(teacher, room). The room change then touches one row, and the timetable read joins the two. The general detector: pick any non-key column and ask 'what decides this value?' If the answer is another non-key column - room is decided by teacher, city by zip, category description by category id - that deciding pair wants its own table. Designs rarely set out to violate this; they grow one 'just add the room, it's right there' column at a time, which is why the detector question belongs in every schema review.
Raw events are 40 million rows a day. A proposal keeps hourly rollups instead of raw events for most queries. Run the storage math and show me what a rollup row looks like.
The arithmetic first, then a rollup built from raw events so the shape is concrete:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, hour TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE hourly_rollup (hour TEXT NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL, n INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (hour, kind))
INSERT INTO hourly_rollup SELECT hour, kind, COUNT(*) FROM events GROUP BY hour, kind
SELECT hour, kind, n FROM hourly_rollup ORDER BY hour, kind

messages.content: Raw volume averages about 1.67 million events per hour; with 12 event kinds, an hourly rollup holds 24 x 12 = 288 rows a day - a reduction factor near 139,000x, which is why rollups exist. The demo rollup shows the shape: one row per (hour, kind) with its count, and every 'how many' question for old data becomes a small SUM over the rollup. What the rollup cannot answer is anything it aggregated away: no per-user journeys, no exact timestamps, no new question sliced by a dimension nobody kept. So the honest architecture is tiered: raw events retained for a window (days or weeks, sized by real re-analysis needs and storage budget), rollups kept forever, and the rollup grain chosen from the questions the business actually asks at age - hour by kind here; if region matters later, region must be in the rollup key from day one, because you cannot re-aggregate what you already threw away. Denormalization by aggregation is a bet about future questions; size the raw window to cover the questions you got wrong.
Support says fixing a customer's address in our system takes 'forever' because the address is copied onto every order. Quantify what they're feeling, then tell me the design answer.
Their complaint is a row count. Counting a rename's blast radius in the copied design, then in the normalized one:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders_flat (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, ship_street TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders_flat VALUES (1, 7, '12 Oak St'), (2, 7, '12 Oak St'), (3, 7, '12 Oak St'), (4, 7, '12 Oak St'), (5, 7, '12 Oak St')
UPDATE orders_flat SET ship_street = '14 Oak St' WHERE customer_id = 7

messages.content: Five demo orders, five rows rewritten for one address change - and that is the small version. At 50,000 historical orders for a long-lived customer, a single 'customer moved' update touches 50,000 rows; at 2 ms of lock and log cost per row that is 100 seconds of write work for a fact that changed once. Worse, most of those writes are wrong to make: yesterday's orders shipped to the old address, and rewriting them falsifies delivery history. The design answer separates the two facts that were sharing a column. The customer's current address lives once in customers (or an addresses table) and updates in one row. Each order carries ship_address_snapshot - the address it actually used - written at order time and never updated. Support's slowness and the audit problem were the same bug: a living fact and a historical fact stored in one place, so maintaining one corrupted the other. When a column is both, split it; the names alone (current_ versus snapshot_) will prevent the next decade of confusion.
Enrollments need more than the pairing now: we record when the student enrolled and their final grade. Does adding attributes change the junction table's key design?
The junction grows columns, but the pair remains the identity - the attributes describe the pairing, not a new entity:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER NOT NULL, course_id INTEGER NOT NULL, enrolled_on TEXT NOT NULL, grade TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id))
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (7, 101, '2026-02-01', 'C')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: enrollments.student_id, enrollments.course_id

arguments.sql: SELECT student_id, grade FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 101 AND grade IS NOT NULL ORDER BY student_id

messages.content: The re-enrollment attempt for (7, 101) is still rejected - enrolled_on and grade did not dilute the key, because they are facts about the pairing: this student enrolled in this course on this date and earned this grade. Grade being NULL until term ends is also honest modeling: the pairing exists before the grade does. The design question to keep asking as attributes accumulate is whether they still describe the pair or have started describing an event. 'Enrolled on' and 'grade' describe the pair. But if a student can drop and re-enroll in the same course next term, the pair stops being unique - then either term joins the primary key, making it (student_id, course_id, term), or the enrollment graduates to an entity with its own id and a lifecycle. Both are respectable; the failure mode is keeping the pair key while quietly allowing duplicates through some side door, because every report that assumes one row per pairing will double-count from that day forward.

Damage claims need to reference 'the third product on shipment 88' - one specific line of a shipment's contents. Our shipment_products junction has a composite key only. Why is that suddenly a problem?
A composite key identifies the line, but nothing else can point at it without copying the whole key - and the pairing has become a thing other facts attach to:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE shipment_lines (line_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, shipment_id INTEGER NOT NULL, product_sku TEXT NOT NULL, qty INTEGER NOT NULL, UNIQUE (shipment_id, product_sku))
INSERT INTO shipment_lines VALUES (1, 88, 'VASE-01', 6), (2, 88, 'BOWL-02', 12), (3, 88, 'MUG-RED', 24)
CREATE TABLE damage_claims (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, line_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES shipment_lines(line_id), units_damaged INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO damage_claims VALUES (1, 3, 2)
SELECT s.shipment_id, s.product_sku, d.units_damaged FROM damage_claims d JOIN shipment_lines s ON s.line_id = d.line_id

messages.content: The claim now references line 3 - 'MUG-RED on shipment 88' - with a single foreign key. This is the graduation pattern for junction tables: while a pairing is only ever traversed (from shipment to products, or product to shipments), a composite key suffices. The moment another table needs to point at the pairing itself - claims against a line, payments against an enrollment, comments on a specific casting of an actor in a film - the pairing is an entity and deserves its own primary key. Keep the UNIQUE(shipment_id, product_sku) constraint when you add the id, exactly as here, so the id becomes a handle, not a license for duplicate lines. The smell that predicts this refactor: a foreign key elsewhere that needs two columns to say which pairing it means, or a developer asking 'but which row of the junction do I attach this to?' Answer that question in the schema, with an id, the first time it is asked.
Prescriptions involve a doctor, a patient, and a drug together - no pair of them means anything alone. How do you model a three-way relationship?
As a junction with three foreign keys, where the triple is the key and the dosage facts hang off it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE prescriptions (doctor_id INTEGER NOT NULL, patient_id INTEGER NOT NULL, drug TEXT NOT NULL, started_on TEXT NOT NULL, dose_mg INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (doctor_id, patient_id, drug))
INSERT INTO prescriptions VALUES (3, 41, 'Lisinopril', '2026-02-01', 10), (3, 42, 'Lisinopril', '2026-02-03', 20), (5, 41, 'Metformin', '2026-01-15', 500)
INSERT INTO prescriptions VALUES (3, 41, 'Lisinopril', '2026-03-01', 15)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: prescriptions.doctor_id, prescriptions.patient_id, prescriptions.drug

arguments.sql: SELECT patient_id, drug, dose_mg FROM prescriptions WHERE doctor_id = 3 ORDER BY patient_id

messages.content: The triple key rejects the second (doctor 3, patient 41, Lisinopril) row: one doctor prescribing the same drug to the same patient twice concurrently is a duplicate fact, not two facts - a dose change is an update (or a history row), not a parallel prescription. Modeling pairwise instead - doctor_patient, patient_drug, doctor_drug tables - would lose exactly the information that matters: it could show that doctor 3 treats patient 41 and that patient 41 takes Lisinopril, but not that doctor 3 prescribed it, which is the only version with legal meaning. The rule: a relationship among N entities is one table with N foreign keys whenever the fact is only true of the whole combination. Check uniqueness semantics before finalizing the key, though: if the same doctor may prescribe the same drug to the same patient again after a gap, started_on joins the key or the prescription takes a surrogate id with an active-period - the medicine decides, the schema just has to ask.
Courses can be prerequisites for other courses - a many-to-many where both sides are courses. Any special dangers in a self-referencing junction?
One table, two foreign keys to the same parent - plus one guard the plain junction does not need:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE prerequisites (course_id INTEGER NOT NULL, requires_id INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (course_id, requires_id), CHECK (course_id <> requires_id))
INSERT INTO prerequisites VALUES (201, 101), (301, 201), (301, 102)
INSERT INTO prerequisites VALUES (101, 101)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: CHECK constraint failed: course_id <> requires_id

arguments.sql: SELECT requires_id FROM prerequisites WHERE course_id = 301 ORDER BY requires_id

messages.content: The self-prerequisite (101 requires 101) is rejected by the CHECK - the one guard a self-junction adds, because 'a thing relates to itself' is usually nonsense in these domains (nobody is their own prerequisite, manager, or follower). The composite key still does its usual work, blocking duplicate edges. What the schema cannot block is a cycle spread across rows: 101 requiring 201 while 201 requires 101 passes every constraint here, because cycle detection is a graph property, not a row property. If cycles would break the domain (prerequisite loops make a degree uncompletable), enforce them at write time with a reachability check - walk the graph from requires_id and refuse the insert if course_id is reachable - in a trigger or the write service. Model the edge table plainly, name the columns by role (course_id versus requires_id, follower versus followee), and remember that in self-referencing junctions the column names carry the meaning the table name no longer can.
We're adding a follow feature: users follow users. Marketing wants to also stop people following themselves via an app-side check. Should the rule live only in the app?
Rules that live only in the app live only in the paths the app remembered. The schema version of the same table:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE follows (follower_id INTEGER NOT NULL, followee_id INTEGER NOT NULL, followed_on TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id), CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id))
INSERT INTO follows VALUES (4, 4, '2026-05-04')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: CHECK constraint failed: follower_id <> followee_id

arguments.sql: INSERT INTO follows VALUES (1, 2, '2026-05-05')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: follows.follower_id, follows.followee_id

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS edges FROM follows

messages.content: Three edges stored; both bad inserts refused without any application involvement - the self-follow by the CHECK constraint, the duplicate follow by the composite primary key. Note the asymmetry the key creates deliberately: (1 follows 2) and (2 follows 1) are different rows, because following is directional; if the domain were mutual friendship instead, you would need a canonical ordering rule (store smaller id first) or a different structure entirely. The reason to duplicate the app-side check in the schema is not distrust of the app - it is that the app is not the only writer the table will ever have. Imports, admin scripts, a second service, a future mobile API: each would need to rediscover every rule. A CHECK and a primary key are the rule stated once, at the only place all writers must pass through. Keep the app check too, for friendly error messages - but let it be a courtesy copy of the schema's law, not the law itself.
A bill of materials needs quantities: a table assembly uses 4 legs and 1 top. A plain two-column junction (assembly, part) can't hold that. What's the right shape?
Quantities are attributes of the pairing, so the junction carries them - and unit consistency becomes part of the design:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bom (assembly TEXT NOT NULL, part TEXT NOT NULL, qty REAL NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), unit TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (assembly, part))
INSERT INTO bom VALUES ('TABLE-A', 'LEG-OAK', 4, 'each'), ('TABLE-A', 'TOP-OAK', 1, 'each'), ('TABLE-A', 'SCREW-M6', 8, 'each'), ('CHAIR-B', 'LEG-OAK', 4, 'each')
SELECT SUM(qty) AS parts_per_table FROM bom WHERE assembly = 'TABLE-A'
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT assembly) AS assemblies_using FROM bom WHERE part = 'LEG-OAK'

messages.content: The junction now answers both directions with quantities: a TABLE-A needs 13 parts in total, and LEG-OAK feeds 2 assemblies - the where-used query that makes a part shortage or a part defect actionable. Two design details matter here. First, qty is REAL with a CHECK (qty > 0) because some pairings are genuinely fractional (0.5 liters of finish per table) while zero or negative quantities are always nonsense; the check encodes that distinction. Second, unit rides along per row because quantity without unit is a number waiting to be misread - if every row in a domain truly shares one unit, the unit can live in documentation, but mixed-unit BOMs (each, liters, meters) must carry it in the data. The general shape: a junction with attributes is still keyed by the pair; attributes like qty, role, position, and since-when are facts about the pairing and belong on the junction row - the moment you catch yourself making a second table 'about' a pairing, the attribute probably just wanted a column here.
Playlist tracks need an order, and users drag tracks to reorder. Our junction is (playlist_id, track_id). Where does position live, and what keeps it consistent?
Position is an attribute of the pairing with its own uniqueness rule - one track per slot, one slot per track:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE playlist_entries (playlist_id INTEGER NOT NULL, track_id INTEGER NOT NULL, position INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (playlist_id, track_id), UNIQUE (playlist_id, position))
INSERT INTO playlist_entries VALUES (5, 91, 1), (5, 92, 2), (5, 93, 3)
INSERT INTO playlist_entries VALUES (5, 94, 2)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: playlist_entries.playlist_id, playlist_entries.position

arguments.sql: SELECT track_id FROM playlist_entries WHERE playlist_id = 5 ORDER BY position

messages.content: Track 94 cannot take position 2 because track 92 already holds it: UNIQUE(playlist_id, position) makes slot collisions impossible, complementing the primary key's guarantee that a track appears once per playlist. The pain arrives at reorder time: moving track 93 to position 1 means renumbering, and naive row-by-row updates collide with the unique constraint mid-shuffle (setting 93 to 1 fails while 91 still holds 1). Practical escapes: update positions in an order that never duplicates (shift the affected range in one UPDATE with position = position + 1, which the engine checks per statement in some databases and per row in others), use sparse positions (10, 20, 30) so inserts and most moves fit between neighbors and renumbering is a rare maintenance job, or drop the unique constraint and let the read side sort by a float position - accepting that the schema no longer guarantees slot integrity. Choose based on how the product behaves: radio-style fixed playlists want strict slots; user playlists usually thrive on sparse positions with an occasional rebalance.
Team membership isn't forever: people join, leave, sometimes rejoin. A plain members junction loses all of that. How should membership be modeled?
By making the junction a history: each membership period is a row, and 'current member' becomes a query, not a flag:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE memberships (team_id INTEGER NOT NULL, person_id INTEGER NOT NULL, joined_on TEXT NOT NULL, left_on TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (team_id, person_id, joined_on))
SELECT person_id FROM memberships WHERE team_id = 2 AND left_on IS NULL ORDER BY person_id
SELECT COUNT(*) AS stints FROM memberships WHERE person_id = 7

messages.content: Person 7 has three stints across two teams and is currently on both team 2 (second stint, left_on NULL) and team 3 - all representable because joined_on joined the primary key, so a rejoin is a new row rather than a resurrection of the old one. The design decisions embedded here: left_on NULL means 'still a member', which makes the current-roster query a simple IS NULL filter; ended stints keep their dates, so 'who was on team 2 last October' is answerable, which a delete-the-row junction could never do. Two integrity gaps remain for the write path to guard, since the schema alone cannot: overlapping stints for the same person and team (a second open row), and left_on earlier than joined_on (a CHECK handles that one - add CHECK (left_on IS NULL OR left_on >= joined_on)). Whenever a relationship has a lifespan the business will ever ask about, model the lifespan from the start; retrofitting history onto a junction that deleted its past is archaeology, not engineering.
The same product sells at different prices in different regions. Is prices(product, region, amount) a junction table or something else?
It wears the junction's shape - two foreign keys and an attribute - and recognizing that shape tells you its key and its queries:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE prices (product_sku TEXT NOT NULL, region TEXT NOT NULL, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0), PRIMARY KEY (product_sku, region))
INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('MUG-RED', 'US', 1200), ('MUG-RED', 'EU', 1350), ('TEA-GRN', 'US', 800)
INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('MUG-RED', 'US', 1250)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: prices.product_sku, prices.region

arguments.sql: SELECT price_cents FROM prices WHERE product_sku = 'MUG-RED' AND region = 'EU'

messages.content: The duplicate (MUG-RED, US) insert is rejected, which is the whole point: for any product and region there is at most one current price, and the pair key enforces it. Structurally this is a junction with an attribute - product and region are the two parents, price is a fact about their combination, not about either alone (the product has no single price; the region has no price at all). Teams sometimes model this as a column per region on the product table (price_us, price_eu), which collapses the day a third region arrives and makes 'list every price under 1000' a cross-column excavation; the row-per-pair shape absorbs new regions as data, not schema changes. The one evolution to anticipate: prices change over time, and the day finance asks 'what was the EU price in March', this table needs effective dates and the pair key grows a from-date - design the current table cleanly now, and that history version is a straightforward extension rather than a rescue.
In a design review, someone calls order_lines 'just a junction table between orders and products'. Is that all it is? I need a clear way to explain the difference.

order_lines starts as a junction and then outgrows the category. The distinction that matters in review:

| Signal | Pure junction (tags on posts) | Junction that became an entity (order_lines) |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning of a row | 'This pair is linked' | 'This order includes this product, this many, at this price' |
| Attributes | None, or nearly | qty, unit price, discount - facts the business computes with |
| Referenced by other tables? | No | Yes - returns, shipments, tax lines point at a line |
| Lifecycle | Exists while the link exists | Has states: shipped, returned, refunded |
| Key | The pair itself | Surrogate id, plus UNIQUE on the pair (and line number) |

The practical rule: a junction stays a junction while its rows are only ever traversed. When rows accumulate attributes that other logic reads, states they move through, or foreign keys pointing at them, you are no longer looking at a link - you are looking at an entity that was born from a relationship. Neither is a failure of the other; the failure is refusing to promote an entity because 'it started as a junction', which leaves claims, returns, and payments trying to reference a pairing that has no handle.
Access control: roles grant capabilities, users hold roles. Most role-capability pairs never exist. Model the grants and show me an effective-permissions lookup.
A sparse junction - only granted pairs get rows - with the permissions check as a three-table join:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE role_grants (role TEXT NOT NULL, capability TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (role, capability))
CREATE TABLE user_roles (user_id INTEGER NOT NULL, role TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (user_id, role))
INSERT INTO role_grants VALUES ('editor', 'publish'), ('editor', 'edit'), ('viewer', 'read'), ('editor', 'read')
INSERT INTO user_roles VALUES (7, 'editor'), (8, 'viewer')
SELECT DISTINCT g.capability FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_grants g ON g.role = ur.role WHERE ur.user_id = 7 ORDER BY g.capability
SELECT COUNT(*) AS can_publish FROM user_roles ur JOIN role_grants g ON g.role = ur.role WHERE ur.user_id = 8 AND g.capability = 'publish'

messages.content: User 7, the editor, effectively holds edit, publish, and read; user 8, the viewer, holds no publish grant - the lookup returns 0, which the app treats as denial. The modeling choices doing the work: absence is meaningful (no row = no grant), so the junction stays sparse and default-deny falls out of the data rather than a flag day of 'granted = 0' rows; and the two junctions compose, so a user's powers are never stored directly - they are always derived from roles, which is what makes 'what changes if we revoke publish from editors' a one-row delete with predictable blast radius. Two cautions from production access systems: first, cache the derived set if checks are hot, but treat the cache as denormalized data with the grants tables as truth; second, if the business ever needs 'grant this one user an exception', resist adding a parallel user_grants table without a precedence rule written down - two sources of permission truth will eventually disagree in the direction you least want.
Org chart: employees have a manager who is also an employee. Model it and show me how we list one manager's direct reports.
The adjacency list - each row points at its parent - is the default hierarchy model, and it answers the one-level question trivially:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id))
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Rae', NULL), (2, 'Ana', 1), (3, 'Bo', 1), (4, 'Cy', 2), (5, 'Dee', 2)
SELECT name FROM employees WHERE manager_id = 1 ORDER BY name
SELECT COUNT(*) AS roots FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL

messages.content: Direct reports of Rae are a single WHERE clause, and exactly one root (manager_id NULL) exists - the CEO. The adjacency list's virtues are real: writes are trivial (a reorg is one UPDATE of manager_id), storage is one column, and one-level questions - the most common in practice - are optimal. Its known limit is everything deeper: 'all reports under Ana, any depth' cannot be expressed with a fixed number of joins, because the depth is data, not schema. That is the fork in hierarchy design: if your questions are mostly one-level plus occasional full-subtree reads, stay with adjacency and add a recursive query (next technique over); if subtree reads are the product - permission inheritance, category rollups, BOM explosions - consider storing the transitive structure explicitly. But never start with the complex model because hierarchies feel scary: most org charts in production are adjacency lists that never needed more.
Staying with the adjacency list for employees - how do we get someone's entire subtree, all levels, without adding columns?
A recursive CTE walks the parent pointers from the top of the subtree down:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id))
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'Rae', NULL), (2, 'Ana', 1), (3, 'Bo', 1), (4, 'Cy', 2), (5, 'Dee', 2), (6, 'Eli', 4)

WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, name, depth) AS (SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE id = 2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, s.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id) SELECT name, depth FROM sub ORDER BY depth, name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	depth
Ana	0
Cy	1
Dee	1
Eli	2

arguments.sql: WITH RECURSIVE sub(id) AS (SELECT id FROM employees WHERE id = 2 UNION ALL SELECT e.id FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id) SELECT COUNT(*) AS subtree_size FROM sub

messages.content: Ana's subtree comes back with depths attached: Ana at 0, Cy and Dee at 1, Eli at 2 - four people including Ana herself. The recursive CTE is the adjacency list's answer to deep reads: no extra storage, no maintenance on writes, and the walk happens at query time. Its costs are equally real: every subtree read re-walks the tree (fine at org-chart scale, painful at million-node category trees read a thousand times a minute), and the query is only as safe as the data - a cycle in manager_id (A manages B manages A) makes the recursion spin until a depth cap stops it, so production recursive queries carry a depth guard and the write path rejects cycles. Choose this when reads are occasional and writes are frequent. When the balance flips - read-heavy, deep, huge - you stop re-deriving the tree on every query and start storing it, which is what closure tables and materialized paths are for.
Category pages need 'everything under Electronics' constantly, plus depth and ancestor checks. A colleague proposes a closure table. What is it and what does it cost?
A closure table stores every ancestor-descendant pair explicitly, trading rows for read speed. Building one for a small tree, then pricing the storage:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE categories (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE category_paths (ancestor_id INTEGER NOT NULL, descendant_id INTEGER NOT NULL, depth INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ancestor_id, descendant_id))
INSERT INTO categories VALUES (1, 'All'), (2, 'Electronics'), (3, 'Audio'), (4, 'Headphones')
SELECT c.name FROM category_paths p JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.descendant_id WHERE p.ancestor_id = 2 AND p.depth > 0 ORDER BY p.depth
SELECT COUNT(*) AS path_rows FROM category_paths

messages.content: Everything under Electronics is now a plain indexed join - Audio at depth 1, Headphones at depth 2 - no recursion, and 'is X under Y' and 'how deep' are single-row lookups. The cost is visible in the count: a 4-node chain needs 10 path rows (every node pairs with itself at depth 0 and with each ancestor), so storage grows with the sum of depths, not the node count. The calculator's scenario - 1,000 categories averaging depth 12 - means roughly 12,000 path rows, which is nothing; but a pathological deep tree turns quadratic-ish, and writes get heavier too: inserting a node writes one path row per ancestor, and moving a subtree rewrites every path through it. Closure tables win when trees are wide and shallow-ish, reads are heavy, and moves are rare - product catalogs are the canonical fit. They lose when the tree churns structurally all day. As ever: the model is a bet about which operations are frequent, priced in rows.
A categories table stores a path string like '1/2/4/' on each row. What queries does that make easy, and where does it bite?
The materialized path: ancestry encoded in a string. Subtree reads become prefix matching:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE categories (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, path TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO categories VALUES (1, 'All', '1/'), (2, 'Electronics', '1/2/'), (3, 'Audio', '1/2/3/'), (4, 'Headphones', '1/2/3/4/'), (5, 'Books', '1/5/')
SELECT name FROM categories WHERE path LIKE '1/2/%' AND id != 2 ORDER BY path
SELECT name FROM categories WHERE path LIKE '1/2/3/%' AND id != 3

messages.content: Everything under Electronics falls out of one LIKE '1/2/%' - Audio and Headphones - and ancestors are just the ids in the string, no joins at all. For read-mostly catalogs this is seductively simple, and the trailing slash matters: it makes '1/2/' a segment boundary, so node 2's prefix cannot accidentally match a node 21 ('1/21/...'). The bites: moving a subtree means rewriting the path of every descendant (the string is denormalized ancestry, with all the update cost that implies); depth and parent are string surgery rather than columns; nothing enforces that the path agrees with reality - a row can claim any ancestry, since there is no parent pointer for a foreign key to check; and sorting by path only matches tree order if segments are zero-padded ('1/10/' sorts before '1/2/' as raw text). Use materialized paths when the tree is small, stable, and read constantly - and keep the parent_id column alongside as the source of truth the path is derived from, so a corrupted path is a rebuild away, not a mystery.
Four ways to store a tree keep coming up in our reviews: adjacency list, closure table, materialized path, nested sets. Give me the comparison I can pin to the wall.

All four store the same tree; they differ in which operations they make cheap and which they make painful.

| Operation | Adjacency list | Closure table | Materialized path | Nested sets (lft/rgt) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Direct children | One indexed lookup | Depth = 1 join | Prefix + depth check | Range + depth check |
| Whole subtree | Recursive CTE walk | One join | One LIKE prefix scan | One BETWEEN range scan |
| Ancestors of a node | Recursive walk up | One join | Parse the path string | Range containment query |
| Insert a leaf | One row | One row per ancestor | One row (compute path) | Renumber many rows |
| Move a subtree | One UPDATE | Rewrite paths through it | Rewrite descendant paths | Renumber much of the tree |
| Extra storage | None | Sum of all depths | One string per node | Two integers per node |
| Integrity enforced by FK | Yes, on parent | Partially | No (string is derived) | No (numbers are derived) |

Default to the adjacency list: it is the only model whose stored form is the fact itself, and modern recursive queries cover occasional deep reads. Promote to a closure table when subtree reads are hot and the tree is wide rather than deep; to a materialized path when reads dominate and the tree barely changes; nested sets only for near-static trees with extreme read-to-write ratios. Whichever you choose, keep parent_id as truth and treat paths, closures, and intervals as derived data you can rebuild.
Our org chart needs 'reports within two levels of a VP' - not the whole subtree, a depth-limited slice. Adjacency list still?
Yes - the recursive walk just carries a depth budget and stops spending it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id))

WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, name, depth) AS (SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE id = 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, s.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id WHERE s.depth < 2) SELECT name, depth FROM sub WHERE depth > 0 ORDER BY depth, name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	depth
A	1
B	1
C	2
D	2
F	2

The slice returns A and B at depth 1, C, D, and F at depth 2 - and stops: E, at depth 3 under C, is excluded because the recursion refuses to extend beyond depth 2. Depth-limited questions are common in real hierarchies (skip-level meetings, approval chains that only climb two rungs, category pages showing two levels of navigation), and the recursive CTE handles them with one extra predicate - no schema change, no derived tables to maintain. This is the adjacency list's home turf: flexible, ad-hoc-shaped reads over a modest tree. The evaluation stays empirical: measure the walk on your real tree. A two-level slice over a 500-person org is microseconds; the same pattern over a 2-million-node taxonomy, run per page view, is where you stop walking and start storing - closure table for the taxonomy, adjacency for the org chart, each where its costs belong.
Reorgs happen quarterly and auditors ask 'who was Pri's manager last March?' Our employees table only has current manager_id. Fix the model.
Manager assignment is a relationship with a lifespan - so it gets the memberships treatment: effective-dated rows, and 'manager on date D' becomes a range query:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE manager_assignments (employee_id INTEGER NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, effective_to TEXT, PRIMARY KEY (employee_id, effective_from))
SELECT manager_id FROM manager_assignments WHERE employee_id = 7 AND effective_from <= '2026-03-15' AND (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to >= '2026-03-15')
SELECT manager_id FROM manager_assignments WHERE employee_id = 7 AND effective_from <= '2026-01-15' AND (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to >= '2026-01-15')

messages.content: Same employee, two dates, two correct answers: manager 5 in mid-March 2026, manager 2 in mid-January - the reorg is preserved instead of overwritten. The pattern is identical to memberships with joined/left dates, because it is the same insight: when a relationship changes over time and anyone will ever ask about the past, the relationship is a table of periods, not a column of current state. The current manager remains available as the row with effective_to IS NULL, so day-to-day queries barely change. What the schema still cannot enforce alone: exactly one open period per employee and no overlapping periods - those are write-path checks (or trigger-enforced, as with price ranges). The employees table keeps a person's stable facts; everything with a lifespan - manager, team, title, location - gets periods. Auditors stop being a special occasion when history is the default shape of change.
Someone created a cycle in our manager data (A's manager is B, B's manager is A) and now the subtree query never terminates. Show me the failure safely and how to prevent it.
The failure, reproduced with a depth cap so it terminates - note the same two people recurring at ever-greater depths:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, manager_id INTEGER REFERENCES employees(id))
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1, 'A', 2), (2, 'B', 1), (3, 'C', 1)
