WITH RECURSIVE sub(id, name, depth) AS (SELECT id, name, 0 FROM employees WHERE id = 1 UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, s.depth + 1 FROM employees e JOIN sub s ON e.manager_id = s.id WHERE s.depth < 6) SELECT name, depth FROM sub ORDER BY depth LIMIT 8

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	depth
A	0
B	1
C	1
A	2
B	3
C	3
A	4
B	5

The walk goes A, then B and C, then A again, then B and C again - without the depth cap it never ends, because the recursion has no way to know it has been here before. No row-level constraint can prevent this: each individual row is legal (A's manager exists; B's manager exists), and the cycle is a property of the graph as a whole. Prevention therefore lives at the write path: before setting X's manager to M, walk up from M - if you reach X, the assignment closes a loop and must be refused. That check belongs in a trigger or the single write service, and it must run on updates as well as inserts, since cycles are usually born in reorgs, not in initial loads. Defense in depth for the read side: every production recursive query carries a depth cap (as here) or a visited-path check, so a bad row degrades into a wrong answer you can investigate rather than a hung query you cannot. Hierarchies feel like simple parent pointers until the first cycle; design for the graph you actually have.
A table assembly contains sub-assemblies which contain parts. Purchasing needs the total count of each leaf part per finished table, with quantities multiplied down the tree. Model and compute it.
A BOM is a hierarchy where edges carry quantities, and the explosion is a recursive walk that multiplies as it descends:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bom (parent TEXT NOT NULL, child TEXT NOT NULL, qty REAL NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (parent, child))
INSERT INTO bom VALUES ('TABLE', 'TOP', 1), ('TABLE', 'LEGSET', 1), ('LEGSET', 'LEG', 4), ('LEGSET', 'BRACE', 2), ('TABLE', 'SCREW', 8), ('LEGSET', 'SCREW', 4)

WITH RECURSIVE boom(node, qty, depth) AS (SELECT child, qty, 1 FROM bom WHERE parent = 'TABLE' UNION ALL SELECT b.child, boom.qty * b.qty, boom.depth + 1 FROM bom b JOIN boom ON b.parent = boom.node WHERE boom.depth < 5) SELECT node, SUM(qty) AS total FROM boom GROUP BY node ORDER BY node

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
node	total
BRACE	2
LEG	4
LEGSET	1
SCREW	12
TOP	1

The explosion multiplies quantities down each path and sums across paths: a TABLE needs 4 LEGs and 2 BRACEs (through LEGSET), 1 TOP, and 12 SCREWs - 8 directly plus 4 more inside the leg set, which is exactly the kind of double-path contribution a naive one-level query misses. This is the adjacency model again - bom(parent, child, qty) is a junction with an attribute, walked recursively - chosen deliberately: BOMs change with engineering revisions, and adjacency makes an edge change a one-row edit. The depth cap is doing safety duty as in the org chart (a part that accidentally contains itself would otherwise recurse forever, and here it would also multiply quantities explosively). If purchasing runs this per order against a huge catalog, the exploded result per finished product is a classic candidate to precompute per revision and store - a snapshot keyed by product and revision - because the inputs change rarely and the multiplication is the same every time. Model for the write pattern, cache for the read pattern.
What are the hierarchy anti-patterns you see most often in schema reviews? I want a list to check ours against.

Five recur constantly. (1) Storing the parent's name or label instead of its id: renames then cascade by hand, and two nodes with the same label ('Miscellaneous' under every department) become indistinguishable. Always reference the parent row, never its display text. (2) Maintaining two representations by hand - a parent_id and a path string (or a depth column) updated in different code paths - until they disagree and nobody knows which is truth. Pick one stored form; derive the rest in queries or rebuildable jobs. (3) Encoding depth as meaning: 'level 2 nodes are regions' breaks the first time someone inserts a grouping level. Depth is a computed property; node type deserves its own column if the business thinks in types. (4) The god-node shortcut: hanging everything off one root row and then special-casing it out of every query. A NULL parent for roots is cleaner than a fake root that reports and permissions must eternally exclude. (5) Assuming the tree is a tree when it is a DAG: a product in two categories, a part in two assemblies, a person with two managers in a matrix org. If a node can legitimately have two parents, a parent_id column is the wrong model entirely - you need an edges table (parent, child) as the primary structure, and all tree techniques become graph techniques. Check for that one first; it invalidates the most design per word.
With a closure table, can we get 'total products in each top-level category, counting everything in its subcategories' in one query? That's the report the catalog team rebuilds in spreadsheets today.
This is the closure table's party trick - the rollup is a join and a GROUP BY, because every descendant path is already stored:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE categories (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, parent_id INTEGER)
CREATE TABLE category_paths (ancestor_id INTEGER NOT NULL, descendant_id INTEGER NOT NULL, depth INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (ancestor_id, descendant_id))
CREATE TABLE products (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, category_id INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO categories VALUES (1, 'All', NULL), (2, 'Electronics', 1), (3, 'Audio', 2), (4, 'Books', 1)

SELECT c.name, COUNT(p.sku) AS products FROM categories c JOIN category_paths cp ON cp.ancestor_id = c.id JOIN products p ON p.category_id = cp.descendant_id WHERE c.parent_id = 1 GROUP BY c.name ORDER BY c.name

messages.content: Books reports 3 products and Electronics reports 3 - two filed directly under it plus both Audio products rolled up through the stored paths, in one grouped query with no recursion and no spreadsheet. This is the workload closure tables exist for: rollup questions over a read-heavy tree, where the answer must include every descendant at any depth. The spreadsheet it replaces was doing this walk by hand, weekly, with stale data. Note the quiet prerequisites that make it trustworthy: the paths table must be maintained on every category insert and move (it is derived data - if a move forgets to rewrite paths, rollups lie confidently), and products point at leaf or any-level categories consistently, since the rollup counts whatever the paths say. If your catalog team asks this question daily, the closure table pays for itself; if they ask it once a quarter, a recursive CTE over the adjacency list answers it with zero extra storage. Same tree, same truth - the frequency of the question picks the model.
We need to move a subtree ('Audio' and everything under it) to a different parent. Compare the write cost in an adjacency list versus a closure table.
Same move, two models. Adjacency first - the move is a single row:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE cat_adj (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, parent_id INTEGER)
INSERT INTO cat_adj VALUES (1, 'All', NULL), (2, 'Electronics', 1), (3, 'Audio', 2), (4, 'Headphones', 3), (5, 'Media', 1)
UPDATE cat_adj SET parent_id = 5 WHERE id = 3
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_under_audio FROM (WITH RECURSIVE s(id) AS (SELECT id FROM cat_adj WHERE id = 3 UNION ALL SELECT c.id FROM cat_adj c JOIN s ON c.parent_id = s.id) SELECT id FROM s)

messages.content: In the adjacency list the entire move - Audio plus Headphones beneath it - is one UPDATE of Audio's parent_id, and the recursive check confirms the subtree (2 nodes) came along intact, because descendants never stored their ancestry. Now the closure-table version of the same move: every path row that passes through Audio must be deleted and re-derived - Audio's rows to its old ancestors, Headphones' rows to its old ancestors, then the new set against Media's ancestry. For this toy tree that is a handful of rows; for a subtree with 500 descendants under a node at depth 6, it is thousands of path rows rewritten in one transaction, with rollup queries reading torn state if the rewrite is not atomic. Neither cost is a defect - they are the two ends of the hierarchy trade: adjacency pays on deep reads, closure pays on structural writes. Catalogs that re-categorize seasonally feel the closure cost a few times a year and the read benefit daily, which is why they still choose closure. Org charts that reorg quarterly and are read one level at a time should stay adjacent. Price your own move frequency before romanticizing either model.

Our customer dimension overwrites segment when it changes (SCD Type 1). Marketing just asked for campaign performance by the segment customers were in last year, and we can't answer. What did Type 1 cost us, and what does Type 2 look like?
Type 1 cost you the past: overwrite means the old segment exists nowhere. Type 2 keeps versions as effective-dated rows:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dim_customer (customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, segment TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, effective_to TEXT, is_current INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, effective_from))
INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (7, 'casual', '2025-01-01', '2025-09-30', 0), (7, 'enthusiast', '2025-10-01', NULL, 1), (9, 'casual', '2025-01-01', NULL, 1)
SELECT segment FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 7 AND effective_from <= '2025-06-01' AND (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to >= '2025-06-01')
SELECT segment FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 7 AND is_current = 1

messages.content: Last June, customer 7 was 'casual'; today they are 'enthusiast' - and both answers are one query away, because the change closed the old row (effective_to set, is_current cleared) and opened a new one instead of overwriting. That is SCD Type 2: versioned rows, a date range each was true, and a current flag for the common case. The costs are honest ones: the dimension grows with change rate, fact tables should reference the version that was current at event time (which is what makes 'sales by segment as it was' exact rather than approximate), and the write path must close-and-open atomically so no instant has zero or two current rows. Type 1 remains right for corrections of errors (a misspelled name was never a 'previous truth') and for attributes nobody will ever analyze historically. The design question is per-attribute, not per-table: for each column ask 'will anyone ever ask what this used to be?' - segment yes, typo'd street name no - and let the answers draw the line.
Product prices change over time and orders must be priced as of their date. Design the price history table and show a point-in-time lookup.
Prices as periods: each row owns a date range, and 'the price on date D' is a range-membership query:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE price_history (sku TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, effective_to TEXT, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (sku, effective_from))
SELECT price_cents FROM price_history WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED' AND effective_from <= '2026-02-15' AND (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to >= '2026-02-15')
SELECT price_cents FROM price_history WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED' AND effective_from <= '2026-05-15' AND (effective_to IS NULL OR effective_to >= '2026-05-15')

messages.content: February's price is 1200, May's is 1500 - same SKU, and the query shape (from <= D and (to is null or to >= D)) is the universal point-in-time pattern you will reuse for manager assignments, memberships, and tax rates. Design notes that matter: ranges here are inclusive on both ends with the next period starting the day after the previous ends; some shops prefer half-open ranges [from, to) with to = next from, which makes adjacency arithmetic cleaner - pick one convention per schema and write it down, because mixing them manufactures one-day gaps and overlaps. NULL effective_to means 'current', which reads naturally but makes uniqueness of the open row a write-path concern. And the invariant this table cannot self-enforce with plain constraints - no overlapping ranges per SKU - is the one to guard in the write service or with a trigger, since two overlapping prices make the point-in-time query return two truths. The lookup is easy; keeping exactly one truth per instant is the design.
With effective-dated rows, how do we guarantee only one 'current' row per customer? A bug just created two current segments for the same customer.
A partial unique index can enforce what a plain unique cannot - uniqueness only among current rows:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dim_customer (customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL, segment TEXT NOT NULL, is_current INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_current_per_customer ON dim_customer (customer_id) WHERE is_current = 1
INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (7, 'casual', 0), (7, 'enthusiast', 1), (9, 'casual', 1)
INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (7, 'collector', 1)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS current_rows_for_7 FROM dim_customer WHERE customer_id = 7 AND is_current = 1

messages.content: The second current row for customer 7 is rejected by the partial unique index, while history rows (is_current = 0) accumulate freely and customer 9's current row is unaffected. This is the enforcement the bug needed: 'at most one current version per entity' is a real invariant of every Type 2 design, and stating it as an index means imports, scripts, and future services all obey it, not just the code path that remembered to close the old row first. Two operational notes. First, the close-and-open update must happen in one transaction - set the old row's is_current to 0 before inserting the new current row, or the index will (correctly) reject your own legitimate change mid-flight. Second, decide whether 'current' is a flag, an effective_to IS NULL sentinel, or a far-future date like 9999-12-31; the flag plus partial index is the most explicit, the sentinel date keeps range queries uniform (no NULL handling), and NULL is the most common but the easiest to make inconsistent with the flag if both exist. One representation of 'current', enforced - not two that can disagree.
Insurance asked: 'What did we believe on March 1 about the address effective in April?' Our address table has only effective dates. Why can't we answer, and what column are we missing?
Because two different times run through every fact: when it was true in the world, and when the system learned it. One timestamp cannot answer questions about the other:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE policy_address (policy_id INTEGER NOT NULL, address TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, recorded_on TEXT NOT NULL)
SELECT address FROM policy_address WHERE policy_id = 55 AND effective_from <= '2026-04-15' AND recorded_on <= '2026-03-01' ORDER BY recorded_on DESC LIMIT 1
SELECT address FROM policy_address WHERE policy_id = 55 AND effective_from <= '2026-04-15' AND recorded_on <= '2026-04-01' ORDER BY recorded_on DESC LIMIT 1

messages.content: As of March 1, the system's belief about April was '14 Oak St' (recorded Feb 10). By April 1 the belief had been corrected to '14 Oak St, Apt 3' (recorded Mar 15) - same effective date, different knowledge. With only effective_from, the correction would have overwritten the earlier belief and the insurer's question - a routine one in regulated industries, asked whenever a claim turns on what was known when - would be unanswerable. This is bitemporal modeling in its smallest useful form: effective time (when the fact holds in the world) plus recorded/system time (when the database held it), with 'what did we believe at time T about time E' answered by filtering both. You do not need it everywhere; you need it wherever decisions are audited against past knowledge - underwriting, billing disputes, clinical and financial records. The cost is that corrections become inserts, never updates, so tables grow and queries carry two range conditions. Pay it exactly where the audit question is real, and keep single-time history everywhere else.
Account balances are computed from an events table (deposits, withdrawals). A teller entered a withdrawal wrong and wants to edit the row. Why do we refuse, and how is it fixed instead?
Because the ledger's value is that it is append-only: corrections are new events that reference the mistake, never edits to it:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE account_events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, kind TEXT NOT NULL, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, reverses_id INTEGER)
INSERT INTO account_events VALUES (1, 3, 'deposit', 10000, NULL), (2, 3, 'withdrawal', -2500, NULL)
INSERT INTO account_events VALUES (3, 3, 'reversal', 2500, 2), (4, 3, 'withdrawal', -2000, 2)
SELECT SUM(amount_cents) AS balance FROM account_events WHERE account_id = 3
SELECT COUNT(*) AS events_kept FROM account_events WHERE account_id = 3

messages.content: Balance 8000 - the wrong 2500 withdrawal was reversed by event 3 (reverses_id pointing at the mistake) and re-entered correctly as event 4 at 2000, and all four events remain on the record. An auditor can replay the whole story: what happened, what was wrong, who fixed it, in what order. Had the teller edited row 2 in place, the balance would be identical today - and the history would be fiction, with no way to answer 'was this account ever debited 2500 in error' or to prove the correction happened after the complaint rather than before it. Append-only ledgers trade a small amount of storage and a slightly harder correction UX for total accountability; balances are always derived by SUM, and if a stored balance cache exists for speed, the event log remains the truth it reconciles against. The rule generalizes beyond money: any table whose past states carry legal or debugging weight should treat UPDATE and DELETE as design smells and corrections as new, linked facts.
We need an audit trail of salary changes: who had what, when it changed. The team proposed updated_at and a 'previous_salary' column. Show me a better mechanism.
A trigger-maintained history table captures every change with no cooperation from application code:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE employees (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, salary_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE salary_history (employee_id INTEGER NOT NULL, old_salary_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, new_salary_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, changed_on TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_hist AFTER UPDATE OF salary_cents ON employees BEGIN INSERT INTO salary_history VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.salary_cents, NEW.salary_cents, '2026-05-01'); END
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (7, 'Ana', 5000000)
UPDATE employees SET salary_cents = 5400000 WHERE id = 7
UPDATE employees SET salary_cents = 5400000 WHERE id = 7
SELECT old_salary_cents, new_salary_cents FROM salary_history WHERE employee_id = 7

messages.content: Two history rows exist: the real change, 5000000 to 5400000, and a no-op 5400000 to 5400000 - the second UPDATE set the salary to its existing value and the trigger still fired, because this engine fires on the UPDATE statement, not on the value actually changing. A production version adds WHEN OLD.salary_cents <> NEW.salary_cents to the trigger so the trail records changes, not attempts; know your engine's behavior here, because audit noise is its own kind of lie. Compare the proposed design: updated_at tells you something changed but not what from; previous_salary remembers exactly one step back and is maintained by whichever code paths remember to. The trigger approach wins on the two properties audit trails live or die by: completeness (every UPDATE passes through it, including scripts and imports) and depth (unbounded history, each row immutable once written). Extend the pattern with a changed_by column fed from a session variable where your engine supports it, and never let the history table be writable by the application role - an audit trail the suspect can edit is a diary, not evidence.
A warehouse design uses SCD Type 3 for region: current_region and previous_region columns. Two moves later, reporting is confused. What does Type 3 actually remember?
Exactly one step back - demonstrated by moving a customer twice and watching the first region fall off the record:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers_t3 (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, current_region TEXT NOT NULL, previous_region TEXT)
INSERT INTO customers_t3 VALUES (7, 'North', NULL)
UPDATE customers_t3 SET previous_region = current_region, current_region = 'South' WHERE id = 7
UPDATE customers_t3 SET previous_region = current_region, current_region = 'West' WHERE id = 7
SELECT current_region, previous_region FROM customers_t3 WHERE id = 7

messages.content: After two moves the row says current 'West', previous 'South' - and 'North' is gone, overwritten by the second shift. That is Type 3's entire contract: it remembers the present and exactly one past, which is genuinely useful for the narrow question it was invented for - 'compare this period under the new assignment versus the old one' - such as sales by current region versus previous region during a territory realignment. It is not a history mechanism, and the confusion came from treating it as one. If the business asks 'what region were they in Q1', Type 3 cannot say after two moves; that question needs Type 2's versioned rows. Choose deliberately: Type 3 when exactly one comparison period matters and the column pair will be dropped after the transition; Type 2 whenever 'used to be' questions have no expiry date. And name the columns honestly (region_before_2026_realign) so a future reader does not mistake a transition aid for an archive.

Sales leadership wants revenue by product category. Products moved categories last year. Finance says the numbers differ depending on how we join. Show me why both answers are 'correct' and which one to report.
The join decides the question: facts keyed to the dimension version current at sale time give as-was; joining to the current version gives as-is:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dim_product (version_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT NOT NULL, category TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO dim_product VALUES (1, 'VASE-01', 'Decor'), (2, 'VASE-01', 'Homeware'), (3, 'MUG-RED', 'Kitchen')
CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, version_key INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_product(version_key), amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT d.category, SUM(s.amount_cents) AS revenue FROM sales s JOIN dim_product d ON d.version_key = s.version_key GROUP BY d.category ORDER BY d.category

SELECT cur.category, SUM(s.amount_cents) AS revenue FROM sales s JOIN dim_product cur ON cur.sku = (SELECT sku FROM dim_product WHERE version_key = s.version_key) AND cur.version_key IN (2, 3) GROUP BY cur.category ORDER BY cur.category

messages.content: As-was: Decor 5000, Homeware 4000, Kitchen 1500. As-is: Homeware 9000, Kitchen 1500. Neither query is buggy - they answer different questions. As-was (the first) preserves what the business looked like when the money arrived: last year's Decor revenue stays Decor, so period comparisons and the reports originally filed remain reproducible. As-is (the second) restates all history under today's org of the catalog: useful for 'how does our current Homeware line perform over time', misleading for 'did Decor meet last year's target'. This is the entire reason Type 2 dimensions give facts a version key: the fact stores which truth it was booked under, and as-is remains computable by joining through to the current version, while the reverse - recovering as-was from a Type 1 dimension - is impossible. Report as-was for accountability and trend honesty; offer as-is as the explicitly labeled management view. When two executives argue over whose number is right, the resolution is almost always naming which question each number answers.
Our point-in-time price query just returned two prices for the same SKU and date - overlapping ranges slipped in. Can the database itself refuse overlaps at insert time?
Plain constraints cannot compare rows, but a trigger can. This one aborts any insert whose range collides with an existing period for the SKU:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE price_history (sku TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, effective_to TEXT, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)

CREATE TRIGGER trg_no_overlap BEFORE INSERT ON price_history BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'overlapping price range') WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM price_history WHERE sku = NEW.sku AND NEW.effective_from <= COALESCE(effective_to, '9999-12-31') AND COALESCE(NEW.effective_to, '9999-12-31') >= effective_from); END
INSERT INTO price_history VALUES ('MUG-RED', '2026-01-01', '2026-03-31', 1200)
INSERT INTO price_history VALUES ('MUG-RED', '2026-04-01', NULL, 1500)
INSERT INTO price_history VALUES ('MUG-RED', '2026-03-15', '2026-05-01', 1300)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS periods FROM price_history WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'

messages.content: The overlapping March-to-May insert is aborted with 'overlapping price range', and the table holds exactly the two legitimate periods. The trigger encodes the invariant the point-in-time query silently assumes: for each SKU, periods partition time - no gaps is a business choice, but no overlaps is a correctness requirement, because an overlap makes 'the price on date D' a plural noun. Note the COALESCE sentinel handling: open-ended rows (effective_to NULL) must compare as infinity, which is the fiddliest part of every range-overlap check and the first place to test. Some databases offer this declaratively (PostgreSQL exclusion constraints over range types) - prefer those where available; the trigger is the portable fallback. Also enforce the same check on UPDATE, not just INSERT, since ranges are usually edited by closing and reopening. A point-in-time design without overlap enforcement is a hope; with it, the query's single-row result is guaranteed by the schema rather than by the care of whoever loaded the prices.
Legal wants us able to erase a customer's personal data on request, but our design keeps immutable history everywhere. Are those irreconcilable?

Not irreconcilable, but the reconciliation has to be designed, not improvised at the first erasure request. The tension is real: history tables, ledgers, and audit trails derive their value from never changing, while erasure rights demand that personal data be removable. Three patterns resolve it in practice. (1) Separate identity from facts: operational and history tables reference a customer by an opaque id, and the mapping from id to name, email, and address lives in one small identity table. Erasure deletes the identity row; the history remains - now about an anonymous id, which preserves aggregates and audit structure while the person is gone. (2) Crypto-shredding: personal fields are encrypted with a per-customer key; erasure destroys the key, rendering every copy - including backups and history - permanently unreadable without touching a row. (3) Tombstoning with redaction: history rows keep their shape but personal fields are overwritten with a marker, accepting that the audit trail now shows 'redacted by request' - the fact of the change is itself part of the record. What does not work: pretending the conflict away, either by refusing erasure because 'the ledger is immutable' or by quietly deleting ledger rows and destroying the audit value. Decide per table which pattern applies while the schema is young; retrofitting erasure onto a design that smeared names and emails across forty history tables is the expensive version of this conversation.
Why do temporal tables so often use (entity_id, effective_from) as the primary key instead of a plain id? Show me what it catches.
Because in a period table, the identity of a row is 'the version of this entity starting at this time' - and the key should say so:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE tax_rates (jurisdiction TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, rate_bp INTEGER NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (jurisdiction, effective_from))
INSERT INTO tax_rates VALUES ('FL', '2026-01-01', 625)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: UNIQUE constraint failed: tax_rates.jurisdiction, tax_rates.effective_from

arguments.sql: SELECT rate_bp FROM tax_rates WHERE jurisdiction = 'FL' AND effective_from <= '2026-03-01' ORDER BY effective_from DESC LIMIT 1

messages.content: The duplicate - a second Florida rate claiming to start 2026-01-01, at a different value - is rejected by the key itself. With a surrogate id it would have sailed in, and the point-in-time lookup ('latest from-date not after the target date', shown here returning 600) would then face two candidates for the same start and pick one arbitrarily. The composite temporal key states the model precisely: one version per entity per start instant. It also clusters the table the way it is read - all versions of one jurisdiction together, ordered by start - so the lookup is a short range scan. A surrogate id still has its place if other tables must reference one specific period (an invoice citing the exact tax-rate row applied); then add the id but keep UNIQUE(jurisdiction, effective_from), the same two-key discipline as entity tables. Keys are claims about identity; in temporal tables the claim includes time, and the schema should make the claim where queries depend on it.

A retroactive correction just landed: March's MUG-RED price was wrong - it should have been 1100, not 1200. Our price_history is effective-dated only. Walk me through handling it without lying about the past.
With only effective time, a correction overwrites what the system believed in March. Adding recorded time lets the correction be a new belief about March, preserving the old one:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE price_history_bt (sku TEXT NOT NULL, effective_from TEXT NOT NULL, effective_to TEXT, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL, recorded_from TEXT NOT NULL, recorded_to TEXT)
INSERT INTO price_history_bt VALUES ('MUG-RED', '2026-03-01', '2026-03-31', 1100, '2026-04-10', NULL)

SELECT price_cents FROM price_history_bt WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED' AND effective_from <= '2026-03-15' AND '2026-03-15' <= effective_to AND recorded_from <= '2026-03-20' AND (recorded_to IS NULL OR recorded_to >= '2026-03-20')
SELECT price_cents FROM price_history_bt WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED' AND effective_from <= '2026-03-15' AND '2026-03-15' <= effective_to AND (recorded_to IS NULL)

messages.content: Two honest answers now coexist. 'What did we believe on March 20 about mid-March prices?' - 1200, the value recorded Feb 20 and not superseded until Apr 10. 'What do we now believe about mid-March?' - 1100, the corrected row. The correction closed the old row's recorded_to rather than deleting it, and inserted the new belief - the bitemporal close-and-open. This is what lets a business reissue March invoices at 1100 while still proving, to an auditor or a customer dispute, that 1200 was the price the system legitimately quoted at the time. In a single-time design you must choose between falsifying history (overwrite to 1100, and March's quotes become inexplicable) and falsifying the present (keep 1200, and every reprint is wrong). Most tables do not need both axes; price, policy, and eligibility data in regulated or dispute-prone domains do. The tell that you need recorded time: someone asks 'when did we find out?' and the answer matters as much as 'when did it change?'
Subscription status changes constantly (trialing, active, past_due, canceled). Billing asks for 'current status' a million times a day and 'status on invoice date' at month end. Model it.
One status-change log serves both: current status is the latest row; historical status is the latest row as of a date:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE status_changes (account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, changed_on TEXT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (account_id, changed_on))
SELECT status FROM status_changes WHERE account_id = 3 ORDER BY changed_on DESC LIMIT 1
SELECT status FROM status_changes WHERE account_id = 3 AND changed_on <= '2026-03-05' ORDER BY changed_on DESC LIMIT 1

messages.content: Current status for account 3: active (recovered on Mar 9). Status on Mar 5: past_due - which is what the invoice issued that week should reflect, and what a dunning dispute will ask about. The change log is the single source; 'current' is a derived view (latest changed_on per account), not a column someone must remember to update in the same breath as inserting the change. If the million-times-a-day read makes the derivation hot, cache current status on the accounts table as denormalized data with the log as truth and a reconciliation that compares them - the same cache discipline as counters and balances. Resist the common alternative of a status column plus a separate history table maintained by application code: two write paths for one fact, and the first time a script updates the column directly, the history silently loses an entry that billing will need at month end. One log, derived presents, reconciled caches - in that order of preference.
Facts arrive before their dimension: tonight's sales reference a customer created in the CRM tomorrow. The load rejects them for a missing customer key. What's the standard escape hatch?
A placeholder dimension row - the 'unknown member' - so facts can land honestly and be re-pointed or reported as pending when the dimension catches up:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE dim_customer (customer_key INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO dim_customer VALUES (-1, 'UNKNOWN - pending CRM'), (101, 'Ana Ruiz')
CREATE TABLE sales (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_key INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES dim_customer(customer_key), amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
SELECT d.name, SUM(s.amount_cents) AS revenue FROM sales s JOIN dim_customer d ON d.customer_key = s.customer_key GROUP BY d.name ORDER BY d.name

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
name	revenue
Ana Ruiz	1850
UNKNOWN - pending CRM	5100

Sales load cleanly: 5100 cents sit against the UNKNOWN member - visible, quantified, and reportable - instead of being rejected into a side file someone forgets, or worse, silently dropped. The placeholder pattern (key -1, sometimes a small set: unknown, not-applicable, late-arriving) is the warehouse's admission that the world is not synchronized. Two disciplines keep it honest: the pending bucket is monitored - a growing UNKNOWN balance is a pipeline bug alarm, not a rounding error - and when the real customer arrives, you choose a policy and write it down: either re-point the facts to the real key (history restated, pending drains to zero) or leave facts as booked and let only new facts use the real member (history preserved as loaded). Both are defensible; drifting between them per incident is not. What the pattern refuses to do is invent a customer or block the load - the fact of the sale is real even when its attribution is temporarily unknown, and the schema should represent 'real but unattributed' as a first-class state.
We keep finding products with negative prices and orders with zero quantity in the database. The app 'validates' these. What should the schema be doing?
App validation is a courtesy; CHECK constraints are the law every writer must obey. Retrofitting the two rules and watching them bite:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0))
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), unit_price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price_cents >= 0))
INSERT INTO products VALUES ('MUG-RED', 1200)
INSERT INTO products VALUES ('BAD-01', -50)
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (1, 0, 1200)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS valid_products FROM products

messages.content: Both bad rows are refused at the database door - negative price, zero quantity - regardless of which code path, import script, or admin console attempted them. The app validation the team relied on only guards the requests that flow through it, in the version that has the check, forever; the first CSV import or hotfix script bypasses it completely. Design guidance for CHECKs: encode invariants that are true by definition of the domain (quantities positive, prices and percentages in range, end dates not before start dates, status among its enumerated values), and keep them cheap and row-local, because cross-row rules do not belong in CHECK. Name your constraints where the engine allows (CHECK (price_cents >= 0) with a name like ck_products_price_nonneg) so the error message a developer sees at 2 a.m. says which law was broken. And keep the app validation too - its job is friendly, immediate feedback; the constraint's job is that the friendly layer is not the only thing between the business and a negative price.

Users who delete their account sometimes re-register with the same email, but our UNIQUE(email) blocks them forever because the deleted row still holds it. We don't want to hard-delete accounts. Solve it in the schema.
Soft delete plus a partial unique index: uniqueness applies only among live accounts:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL, deleted_at TEXT)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_live_email ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'kim@x.com', NULL)
UPDATE users SET deleted_at = '2026-04-01' WHERE id = 1
INSERT INTO users VALUES (2, 'kim@x.com', NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (3, 'kim@x.com', NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS live_accounts FROM users WHERE email = 'kim@x.com' AND deleted_at IS NULL

messages.content: The story in four acts: the original account registers; it soft-deletes (deleted_at set, row retained for order history and audit); re-registration with the same email succeeds, because the partial index only governs rows where deleted_at IS NULL; and the third insert - a second live account with that email - is rejected, because among live accounts the email is still unique. Exactly one live account holds the email, which is the real business rule; the naive UNIQUE(email) overstated it as 'one account ever, across all time', confusing an identity rule with a history rule. Partial indexes are the general tool whenever a constraint's scope is a subset: one current row per entity, one active subscription per customer, unique slugs among non-archived posts. Two cautions: every query and ORM mapping must respect the same deleted_at convention or the undead rows leak into reports, and if your engine lacks partial indexes, the fallback is a generated column that is the email when live and NULL when deleted, with a plain unique index over it (NULLs do not collide). Either way, state the rule where the data lives.
Deleting a customer who has orders fails; deleting one with only login sessions works and nulls them. Both behaviors were 'designed'. Explain the menu of delete rules and how to choose.
Every foreign key carries an ON DELETE decision, whether or not anyone remembers making it. The two contrasting cases:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT)
CREATE TABLE sessions (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, device TEXT)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1, 'Ana'), (2, 'Bo')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10, 1)
INSERT INTO sessions VALUES (100, 2, 'phone'), (101, 1, 'laptop')
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 1
DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 2
SELECT customer_id FROM sessions WHERE id = 100

messages.content: Deleting Ana (id 1) fails: RESTRICT on orders says a customer with order history cannot vanish - the orders are financial records that must keep their owner. Deleting Bo (id 2) succeeds, and his session's customer_id becomes NULL: sessions are ephemeral, and SET NULL says 'the session may outlive its owner as an anonymous artifact' (or would, in a design that keeps them at all). The menu: RESTRICT/NO ACTION - the parent is load-bearing, deletion is a business process, not a row operation; CASCADE - the children are existentially part of the parent (order lines die with their order; a user's draft posts with their account); SET NULL - the child survives meaningfully without the parent, and the FK column must be nullable for it to be legal. Choose per relationship by asking 'if this parent goes, what is this child?' Part of it: cascade. Record about it: restrict. Independent thing that merely referenced it: null or restrict, decided by whether an orphan still means anything. The dangerous delete rule is the default you never chose - make every FK's behavior an explicit line in the schema review.
Regions are identified by a two-letter code used as a key across twelve tables. The business is renaming region 'NW' to 'PNW'. How bad is this, and what setting decides it?
It depends entirely on whether the foreign keys were declared ON UPDATE CASCADE. With it, the rename is one statement:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE regions (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE stores (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, region_code TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES regions(code) ON UPDATE CASCADE)
INSERT INTO regions VALUES ('NW', 'Northwest'), ('SE', 'Southeast')
INSERT INTO stores VALUES (1, 'NW'), (2, 'NW'), (3, 'SE')
UPDATE regions SET code = 'PNW' WHERE code = 'NW'
SELECT COUNT(*) AS stores_repointed FROM stores WHERE region_code = 'PNW'

messages.content: One update, two stores repointed automatically, zero orphaned rows - ON UPDATE CASCADE turned a twelve-table migration into a non-event. Without it, the same rename is blocked by every referencing row, and the team ends up doing the disable-checks, update-everything-in-the-right-order, re-enable dance under time pressure. But treat this as a story with two morals, not one. First moral: if you use natural keys that can change, declare the cascade - it is the seatbelt for exactly this accident. Second moral, deeper: a key that the business renames for branding reasons was carrying meaning, and meaning is what changes. 'NW' to 'PNW' is the email-as-primary-key lesson wearing a shorter coat. The robust long-term shape is a surrogate region id that never changes, the code as a unique display attribute that can be renamed with a one-row update touching nothing else. Cascades make natural-key changes survivable; surrogates make them trivial. If you inherit the former, declare the cascade today, before the next rebrand, not during it.

We need to insert an order line before its order header exists (the integration sends children first), inside one transaction. Foreign keys keep rejecting it. Is there a legitimate mechanism, or must we reorder the feed?
Deferred constraints: the FK is still enforced, but at commit time instead of statement time. The feed's order stops mattering inside the transaction:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, note TEXT)
CREATE TABLE order_lines (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED, sku TEXT)
BEGIN
INSERT INTO order_lines VALUES (1, 500, 'MUG-RED')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (500, 'header arrives second')
COMMIT
SELECT COUNT(*) AS lines_stored FROM order_lines WHERE order_id = 500

messages.content: The line lands and commits, because DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED moved the check to COMMIT, by which time the header exists. Had the transaction ended without the header, the commit itself would fail and roll back - the invariant is identical, only its timing changed. Legitimate uses are narrow and specific: bulk loaders and integrations whose record order you do not control, cyclic references between two tables that must be inserted together, and ORM unit-of-work patterns that flush in arbitrary order. The costs argue for restraint: errors surface at commit, far from the statement that caused them, which makes debugging and user-facing error messages harder; some engines restrict what deferred constraints can do (and deferrable unique constraints interact with upserts in surprising ways). Default remains immediate enforcement - fail fast, at the offending line, is a feature. Reach for deferral when the write pattern is provably order-hostile, document it on the constraint, and make sure the integration's transaction boundaries are real - a deferred check across an autocommit boundary is just a delayed failure with worse diagnostics.
Inventory must never go negative, but the rule spans rows: a shipment is valid only if the product's total stock covers it. CHECK can't see other rows. Enforce it anyway.
A trigger that computes the resulting balance and aborts the insert if it would cross zero:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE stock_moves (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, sku TEXT NOT NULL, delta INTEGER NOT NULL)

CREATE TRIGGER trg_no_negative BEFORE INSERT ON stock_moves BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'insufficient stock') WHERE (SELECT COALESCE(SUM(delta), 0) FROM stock_moves WHERE sku = NEW.sku) + NEW.delta < 0; END
INSERT INTO stock_moves VALUES (1, 'MUG-RED', 100)
INSERT INTO stock_moves VALUES (2, 'MUG-RED', -70)
INSERT INTO stock_moves VALUES (3, 'MUG-RED', -40)
INSERT INTO stock_moves VALUES (4, 'MUG-RED', -30)
SELECT SUM(delta) AS on_hand FROM stock_moves WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'

messages.content: The -40 shipment is aborted with 'insufficient stock' (only 30 remained after the first two moves), the -30 that exactly empties the shelf is allowed, and on-hand ends at exactly 0 - never below. This is the standard escalation ladder for invariants: CHECK for rules within a row, UNIQUE for rules within a column set, foreign keys for rules between two tables, and triggers for rules over aggregates and other rows. Two honest warnings about trigger-enforced aggregate rules. First, concurrency: two simultaneous shipments can both read a sufficient balance and both pass, overdrawing in concert - under real contention this check needs to live inside a serialized transaction or be restructured as an UPDATE of a stock counter with a CHECK (stock >= 0) on the counter row, which the engine can enforce atomically. Second, performance: the trigger sums the ledger per insert, which is fine at this scale and a design smell at millions of moves - another argument for the counter-row pattern at volume. Choose the mechanism your concurrency and scale demand, but choose one at the data layer: 'the app checks stock first' is a race condition with a UI.
A room-booking table keeps accepting double bookings: same room, overlapping times, different people. Rows each look valid. How do we make overlap impossible in the schema?
Overlap is a relationship between rows, so again a trigger does what CHECK cannot - comparing the new range against its neighbors, with touching boundaries allowed:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE bookings (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, room TEXT NOT NULL, starts_at TEXT NOT NULL, ends_at TEXT NOT NULL, CHECK (ends_at > starts_at))

CREATE TRIGGER trg_no_double_book BEFORE INSERT ON bookings BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'room already booked') WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bookings WHERE room = NEW.room AND NEW.starts_at < ends_at AND NEW.ends_at > starts_at); END
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, 'Studio B', '2026-05-02 10:00', '2026-05-02 11:00')
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (2, 'Studio B', '2026-05-02 11:00', '2026-05-02 12:00')
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (3, 'Studio B', '2026-05-02 10:30', '2026-05-02 11:30')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS bookings_kept FROM bookings

messages.content: Two bookings kept: the 10:00-11:00 and the back-to-back 11:00-12:00 (touching is not overlapping - the strict inequalities in the overlap test are doing precise work), while the 10:30-11:30 that straddles both is aborted with 'room already booked'. The overlap predicate (new.start < existing.end AND new.end > existing.start) is worth memorizing; every 'mostly overlapping' hand-rolled version of it leaks an edge case, usually the fully-contained or exactly-adjacent one. The CHECK on ends_at > starts_at handles the degenerate row, the trigger handles the relational rule, and the same concurrency caveat as all trigger checks applies: two simultaneous inserts can both see a free room, so high-contention booking systems serialize per room or use an engine with exclusion constraints (PostgreSQL's EXCLUDE over a time range is exactly this rule, declarative and race-safe). Also apply the trigger to UPDATE - moving a booking is just an insert wearing a disguise. Double bookings are never a UI problem; they are a missing invariant, and invariants belong where all writers must pass.
A report undercounted: WHERE NOT (is_member = 1) returned fewer rows than expected - members and non-members don't add up to the total. The column allows NULLs. What's the schema lesson?
NULL is not false, and three-valued logic just taxed the report. Counting the three populations explicitly:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE contacts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, is_member INTEGER)
INSERT INTO contacts VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 0), (4, NULL), (5, NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS flagged_member FROM contacts WHERE is_member = 1
SELECT COUNT(*) AS not_flagged FROM contacts WHERE NOT (is_member = 1)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unknown FROM contacts WHERE is_member IS NULL

messages.content: Members 2, NOT(members) 1, total 5 - the two NULL rows vanished from both sides, because is_member = 1 is neither true nor false for them; it is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true. The schema lesson is to decide, per column, whether 'unknown' is a real state of your domain. For a flag like is_member it almost never is: a contact either is a member or is not, so the column should be INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 with a CHECK (is_member IN (0,1)), making every row decidable and every report add up. Reserve NULL for genuine absence-of-fact: a delivery date for an unshipped order, a left_on for a current member, a middle name. The design review question is 'what does NULL mean here, in business words?' If nobody can say it in business words, the column is nullable by accident and will tax every future query with three-valued surprises. NOT NULL by default, NULL by deliberate exception - and where NULL is used, its meaning goes in the schema documentation next to the column, because every report writer will have to handle it forever.
Order status can be 'draft', 'paid', 'shipped', 'canceled'. One team wants CHECK (status IN (...)), another wants a status lookup table with a foreign key. Settle it with evidence.
Both enforce the same rule today. They differ the day the business adds a status - which is an ALTER in one design and an INSERT in the other:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE statuses (code TEXT PRIMARY KEY, label TEXT NOT NULL, is_terminal INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO statuses VALUES ('draft', 'Draft', 0), ('paid', 'Paid', 0), ('shipped', 'Shipped', 0), ('canceled', 'Canceled', 1)
CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, status TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES statuses(code))
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 'paid')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (2, 'refunded')
INSERT INTO statuses VALUES ('refunded', 'Refunded', 1)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (2, 'refunded')
SELECT COUNT(*) AS orders_now FROM orders

messages.content: The mistyped 'refunded' was rejected by the foreign key while the lookup lacked it, then accepted after a one-row INSERT added the status - no schema change, no deployment, and the new status arrived carrying its own metadata (label, is_terminal). That metadata is the real decider. A status in a real system is never just a string: it has a display label, a sort order, terminal/non-terminal behavior, whether it triggers emails, whether it counts as revenue. The moment any of those questions exist, the lookup table wins, because the CHECK design would scatter those facts across application code. The CHECK wins in the opposite world: a truly closed, tiny, specification-fixed set (cardinal directions, ISO weekday numbers) where adding a value is a design change anyway and a join is pure overhead. Also note the hybrid most mature schemas land on: lookup table for the domain data, plus the foreign key doing enforcement - the table is the constraint. What to avoid is the third option teams drift into: a free-text status column with a wiki page listing the allowed values. That is not a design; it is a rumor with a column.

We have UNIQUE(tenant_id, email) on users... actually no - we have UNIQUE(email) globally, but the product is multi-tenant and the same email legitimately exists in different tenants. Also someone found two rows with the same (account, external_ref) where external_ref was NULL. Two uniqueness bugs - explain both.
Uniqueness rules must match the scope of identity - and NULL quietly opts out of uniqueness in most engines. The NULL hole first:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE imports (account_id INTEGER NOT NULL, external_ref TEXT, UNIQUE (account_id, external_ref))
INSERT INTO imports VALUES (5, 'EXT-1'), (5, NULL), (5, NULL)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_for_account FROM imports WHERE account_id = 5

messages.content: Three rows sit in account 5, two of them with external_ref NULL - the unique constraint never fired, because in standard SQL semantics NULL is not equal to anything, not even another NULL, so (5, NULL) and (5, NULL) are not duplicates as the constraint sees it. Teams discover this in imports and idempotency keys, where NULL means 'no reference supplied' and duplicates pile up silently. Fixes: make the column NOT NULL with a sentinel if 'none' is a real state; add a partial unique index covering the NULL case; or index a generated column COALESCE(external_ref, '') so absence becomes a comparable value. The tenant bug is the mirror image: a global UNIQUE(email) asserts email identifies a person across the whole product, but in a multi-tenant system identity is scoped - the same email is a different account in each tenant, so the constraint must be UNIQUE(tenant_id, email), and every key and lookup in the system inherits that scoping. Both bugs are the same design error in opposite directions: the constraint stated a scope the domain does not have (too narrow, letting NULLs slip; too wide, banning legitimate rows). Uniqueness is always 'unique within what, counting what as equal' - answer both halves explicitly.
For design reviews: a one-page comparison of the constraint mechanisms - what each one can and cannot enforce.

Match the mechanism to the shape of the rule; using a weaker one than the rule needs is how bad data gets in.

| Mechanism | Enforces | Cannot enforce | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| NOT NULL | A value is always present | Anything about the value | email must be supplied |
| CHECK (row-local) | Rules within one row | Comparisons across rows | qty > 0; ends_at > starts_at |
| PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE | No duplicates in a column set | Rules involving NULLs (they slip past); conditional scope | one account per email |
| Partial unique index | Uniqueness within a subset | Rules outside the subset | one live account per email; one current row per entity |
| FOREIGN KEY | Referenced row exists; delete/update behavior | Rules about the referenced row's values | every order has a customer |
| Trigger | Cross-row and aggregate rules | Nothing in principle - but concurrency and performance are on you | no overlapping bookings; stock never negative |
| Application validation | Friendly, immediate feedback | Anything, once another writer exists | form hints, format suggestions |

Two review habits follow. First, for every business rule spoken aloud in a design session, name the mechanism from this table that will hold it - if the answer is 'the app checks', the rule is unenforced. Second, prefer the highest (most declarative) mechanism that can express the rule: a CHECK is self-documenting and optimizer-visible, a trigger is neither. Escalate down the table only when the rule's shape forces you to.

After a customer merge, an engineer 'cleaned up' by setting customer_id to NULL on the merged customer's old orders instead of repointing them. The FK allowed NULLs. Revenue by customer now underreports and nobody can reconstruct attribution. What went wrong at design time?
The orders table said, in schema, that an order may have no customer. For financial history that sentence is false - and the cleanup exploited the permission:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER, amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 7, 4200), (2, 7, 1850), (3, 8, 990)
UPDATE orders SET customer_id = NULL WHERE customer_id = 7
SELECT COUNT(*) AS unattributed_orders FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL
SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_cents), 0) AS unattributed_cents FROM orders WHERE customer_id IS NULL

messages.content: Two orders and 6050 cents are now unattributed - not deleted, just permanently unowned, and no query can restore which customer they belonged to. The design-time error was a nullable foreign key on a relationship that is not optional: an order cannot exist without a customer, so customer_id should have been NOT NULL with ON DELETE RESTRICT, making both this cleanup and accidental orphaning impossible at the schema level. Merges then have exactly one legal shape: repoint the orders to the surviving customer (UPDATE ... SET customer_id = survivor), ideally recording the merge in a merge_log (loser_id, survivor_id, merged_on) so attribution history stays explainable. The broader principle: nullability of a foreign key is a modeling claim - 'this relationship is optional' - and it should be as deliberate as the relationship itself. Shopping carts may lack a customer (guest checkout); orders may not. Drafts may lack a category; published posts may not. In review, read every nullable FK aloud as 'a X may have no Y' and make the room agree with the sentence. Where they cannot, NOT NULL is the fix, and it is much cheaper before the first cleanup than after it.
Inventory oversells keep happening: stock shows 3, two clerks sell 3 each. The app reads stock, checks, then decrements. Where should this rule actually live?
Read-check-write in the app is a race. Moving the rule into the data layer - a counter column whose CHECK makes the oversell unrepresentable:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE stock (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, on_hand INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (on_hand >= 0))
INSERT INTO stock VALUES ('MUG-RED', 3)
UPDATE stock SET on_hand = on_hand - 3 WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'
UPDATE stock SET on_hand = on_hand - 3 WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'
SELECT on_hand FROM stock WHERE sku = 'MUG-RED'

messages.content: The first sale drains stock to 0; the second update is rejected outright - not by a lock or a retry loop, but because the resulting state (-3) violates CHECK (on_hand >= 0), and the engine evaluates that atomically with the write. Compare the app pattern: both clerks read 3, both see 'enough', both decrement - the check and the write were separate instants, and the race lived in the gap. Collapsing them into a single conditional UPDATE (decrement only the row, let the constraint judge the result) removes the gap entirely; the application just reports 'insufficient stock' when its update fails or affects zero rows (a WHERE on_hand >= requested variant achieves the same with a friendlier signal). The design moral generalizes to balances, seats remaining, and budget caps: any invariant of the form 'this number must not cross a line' belongs on the number itself as a constraint, updated by atomic single statements. Checks performed by reading and then writing in application code are not controls; they are observations, and under concurrency they observe a world that no longer exists.

We added CHECK (email LIKE '%@%.%') to stop junk emails. It stopped some. Then 'a@b.c' sailed through, and a valid address with no dot in the domain (intranet) got rejected. What are CHECK format rules actually good for?
Watching the pattern be simultaneously too weak and too strong - which is the fate of most format constraints:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE signups (email TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (email LIKE '%@%.%'))
INSERT INTO signups VALUES ('real.person@example.com')
INSERT INTO signups VALUES ('a@b.c')
INSERT INTO signups VALUES ('no-at-sign.com')

messages.name: database_query
messages.content: Error: CHECK constraint failed: email LIKE '%@%.%'

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS accepted FROM signups

messages.content: Two accepted: the real address and 'a@b.c', which satisfies the pattern while being nearly content-free; the no-@ junk was refused; and the intranet address from the report would be refused too, despite being deliverable in its world. This is the honest scope of format CHECKs: they enforce shape, never truth. An email's real validity is established by sending mail to it (confirmation loops), a phone's by calling it, a SKU's by it existing in the catalog (a foreign key - note how existence beats pattern). Use format constraints for cheap, stable, structural facts you are sure of: a country code is two letters, a percentage sits between 0 and 100, a timestamp's end follows its start. The failure mode to avoid is escalating the pattern war - each junk example inspires a longer LIKE or a regex, each regex rejects a new class of legitimate input, and the constraint slowly becomes a wrong theory of the domain enforced at gunpoint. When a 'format' rule keeps growing exceptions, that is the signal the property was never structural; move validation to the process that can actually verify the thing, and let the schema keep only the invariants that are true by definition.
We need orders.customer_email to become NOT NULL with real values for 2 million existing rows, mid-flight, no downtime window. Walk me through the safe sequence on a small scale.
Expand, backfill, verify, enforce - in that order, never in one heroic ALTER:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE customers (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (7, 'ana@x.com'), (8, 'bo@x.com')
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 7), (2, 8), (3, 7)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN customer_email TEXT
UPDATE orders SET customer_email = (SELECT email FROM customers WHERE customers.id = orders.customer_id)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS still_null FROM orders WHERE customer_email IS NULL

messages.content: The sequence, each step safe to run while the old code is live: (1) expand - ADD COLUMN customer_email as nullable, which is instant and breaks nothing; (2) dual-write begins in the application (new orders write both customer_id and email) so the backfill is chasing a shrinking gap, not a moving flood; (3) backfill existing rows from the customers table, in batches at production scale; (4) verify - the still_null count reads 0, the gate that must pass before enforcement; (5) contract - enforce NOT NULL (in engines without a direct alter, via a validated CHECK (customer_email IS NOT NULL) first, then a table rebuild in a maintenance moment), and only later drop the old column once no reader uses it. The two failure modes this choreography exists to prevent: enforcing before backfilling (the migration fails or locks the table scanning for violations at the worst moment) and dropping the old shape before every deployed reader has moved (the previous app version is still serving traffic during the rollout). Expand-and-contract feels slow; it is the speed at which production schemas are allowed to change.
The backfill for a new column has 40 million rows to fill. The first attempt ran as one giant UPDATE and locked the table for an hour. Show me the batched pattern.
Small transactions, each claiming a bounded slice by key range, resumable and throttleable:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE events (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, kind TEXT NOT NULL, kind_code INTEGER)
INSERT INTO events VALUES (1, 'click', NULL), (2, 'buy', NULL), (3, 'click', NULL), (4, 'view', NULL), (5, 'buy', NULL), (6, 'click', NULL), (7, 'view', NULL)
UPDATE events SET kind_code = CASE kind WHEN 'click' THEN 1 WHEN 'buy' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM events WHERE kind_code IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 3)
UPDATE events SET kind_code = CASE kind WHEN 'click' THEN 1 WHEN 'buy' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM events WHERE kind_code IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 3)
UPDATE events SET kind_code = CASE kind WHEN 'click' THEN 1 WHEN 'buy' THEN 2 ELSE 3 END WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM events WHERE kind_code IS NULL ORDER BY id LIMIT 3)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS remaining FROM events WHERE kind_code IS NULL

messages.content: Three batches of at most 3 rows: 3 affected, 3 affected, 1 affected, then zero remaining - the loop's termination signal is an UPDATE that touches 0 rows. Scaled to 40 million, each batch is its own short transaction: locks are held for milliseconds, replication lag stays bounded, the job can pause between batches if production load spikes, and if it crashes at batch 9,000 it resumes from the remaining NULLs rather than from zero, because 'kind_code IS NULL' is both the work queue and the progress marker. The giant single UPDATE failed on every one of those axes: one transaction, one hour-long lock, all-or-nothing. Two refinements for real scale: order batches by primary key so the scan is sequential and the cache behavior sane, and add a small sleep or lag check between batches - a backfill is a background citizen, and its politeness is measured in the p99 latency of the queries sharing the table. Idempotence is the design principle: a batch that can be safely re-run needs no bookkeeping about where it stopped.
We want to rename orders.total to orders.total_cents for clarity. A rename seems trivial - why did the last one cause an outage?
Because a rename is a breaking change for every reader compiled against the old name. The break, then the rename-that-isn't: expand with a sync trigger so both names live during the transition:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total INTEGER NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1, 4200), (2, 1850)
SELECT total_cents FROM orders WHERE id = 1
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN total_cents INTEGER
UPDATE orders SET total_cents = total
CREATE TRIGGER trg_orders_sync AFTER UPDATE OF total ON orders BEGIN UPDATE orders SET total_cents = NEW.total WHERE id = NEW.id; END
UPDATE orders SET total = 5000 WHERE id = 1
SELECT total, total_cents FROM orders WHERE id = 1

messages.content: The direct query against total_cents failed before the column existed ('no such column') - that error, served to production traffic, is the outage shape: during a rolling deploy, old and new app versions coexist, and a rename instantly orphans whichever version still speaks the old name. The safe rename is really an expand-contract in miniature: add total_cents alongside total, backfill it, keep the two synchronized (a trigger here; dual-writes in the app work too, with the trigger safer because it covers every writer), deploy readers to the new name, wait until the old name has no readers - check logs, not hopes - then drop total in a later change. Yes, it is five steps for a rename. The counter-argument to keep in your pocket: if the name is merely ugly but unambiguous, the cheapest correct migration is none. Renames earn their choreography when the old name is actively misleading (total that is sometimes dollars, sometimes cents - exactly the ambiguity the _cents suffix exists to kill), not when it is merely unfashionable.
We're splitting email out of users into a contacts table during a live migration. During the transition, writes must land in both places or readers of the new table see stale data. How?
A sync trigger on the old table keeps the new table current for every writer, including ones nobody told about the migration:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE contacts (user_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana@x.com'), (2, 'bo@x.com')
INSERT INTO contacts SELECT id, email FROM users
CREATE TRIGGER trg_users_email_sync AFTER UPDATE OF email ON users BEGIN UPDATE contacts SET email = NEW.email WHERE user_id = NEW.id; END
UPDATE users SET email = 'ana@new.com' WHERE id = 1
SELECT email FROM contacts WHERE user_id = 1

messages.content: Ana's email changed in users, and contacts - the table new code reads - already says ana@new.com, because the trigger propagated the write the instant it happened. This is the dual-write pattern with the second write moved into the database, which is the only place that sees all writers: the legacy app, the new service, the admin script, the one cron job everyone forgot. Application-level dual-writes fail precisely on the forgotten writer. The migration then proceeds in the usual expand-contract rhythm: backfill contacts from users (done above), sync trigger on, flip reads to contacts, flip writes to contacts (with a reverse trigger if old readers remain), and finally drop the column from users when the last old reader retires. Two cautions: triggers that write other tables must be part of the schema's documented design, not folklore - name them systematically and list them in the migration runbook; and every sync trigger needs a retirement date in the plan, because a forgotten sync trigger becomes a haunted house - writes propagating to a table nobody owns anymore, long after the migration it served is forgotten.
Prices were stored as TEXT dollars ('19.99') in a legacy column. We're moving to integer cents in a rebuilt table. Show the migration and how we prove nothing was lost or altered.
Rebuild-style migration: create the new shape, transform on the way across, and reconcile totals before the swap:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE products_old (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, price_text TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE products_new (sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY, price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents >= 0))
INSERT INTO products_new SELECT sku, CAST(ROUND(CAST(price_text AS REAL) * 100) AS INTEGER) FROM products_old
SELECT sku, price_cents FROM products_new ORDER BY sku

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
sku	price_cents
A	1999
B	10
C	12000
D	750

arguments.sql: SELECT SUM(price_cents) AS new_total_cents FROM products_new

messages.content: The new table reads 1999, 10, 12000, 750 - and the independent sum, 14759 cents, matches the calculator's hand total of the four prices converted by eye. That reconciliation is the migration's proof: row counts equal, sum of values equal (computed by two independent paths - SQL over the new table, arithmetic over the source values), and spot rows verified. The ROUND inside the transform is load-bearing, not decorative: '19.99' parsed as a float and multiplied by 100 is 1998.9999..., and a bare CAST would truncate it to 1998 - a one-cent corruption on exactly the prices that look most ordinary, repeated across the catalog. This is why money migrates to integer minor units and why float arithmetic anywhere near currency is a defect, not a style choice. After reconciliation: swap table names in a transaction where the engine allows, keep products_old renamed (not dropped) for one release cycle as the rollback path, and let the CHECK on the new column stand guard so the class of error that created TEXT prices cannot re-enter through the new door.
users.name holds full names; the new design wants first_name and last_name. Migrate the data, and be honest about the rows that don't fit the assumption.
Splitting on the first space with INSERT ... SELECT string surgery - and surfacing the edge cases instead of hiding them:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users_old (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users_old VALUES (1, 'Ana Ruiz'), (2, 'Bo Lindqvist'), (3, 'Madonna'), (4, 'Mary Jane Watson')
CREATE TABLE users_new (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, first_name TEXT NOT NULL, last_name TEXT NOT NULL)

INSERT INTO users_new SELECT id, CASE WHEN instr(name, ' ') > 0 THEN substr(name, 1, instr(name, ' ') - 1) ELSE name END, CASE WHEN instr(name, ' ') > 0 THEN substr(name, instr(name, ' ') + 1) ELSE '' END FROM users_old
SELECT id, first_name, last_name FROM users_new ORDER BY id

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
id	first_name	last_name
1	Ana	Ruiz
2	Bo	Lindqvist
3	Madonna	
4	Mary	Jane Watson

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS needs_review FROM users_new WHERE last_name = ''

messages.content: The split lands as: Ana / Ruiz, Bo / Lindqvist, Madonna / (empty), Mary / Jane Watson. Two of those are judgment calls wearing a mechanical costume - 'Madonna' has no last name to extract (empty string, flagged by the needs_review count of 1), and 'Mary Jane Watson' split after the first space, though her first name is arguably 'Mary Jane'. No string function can resolve those; they are semantic, and the migration's job is to route them to human review rather than pretend the transform was lossless. Design the migration accordingly: run the mechanical split, emit the exception report as a first-class output (rows with no space, rows with multiple spaces, suspiciously long last names), and get sign-off on the exceptions before cutover. Also keep the original name column (or the whole old table) until the new shape has survived a release cycle - name data is identity data, and 'we can re-derive it' is false comfort once the source is dropped. Column splits are never just type changes; they are claims about the structure of the data, and every claim has counterexamples living in the table already.

Two legacy tables, customers_a (from the shop) and customers_b (from support), both have customers with overlapping emails. Merge them into one table without duplicating people or losing rows silently.
Union with a stated dedupe rule - email is the match key, source A wins - and counts that prove what happened to every row:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE customers_a (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
CREATE TABLE customers_b (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers_a VALUES ('ana@x.com', 'Ana Ruiz'), ('bo@x.com', 'Bo Lind')
INSERT INTO customers_b VALUES ('bo@x.com', 'B. Lind (support)'), ('cy@x.com', 'Cy Young')
CREATE TABLE customers (email TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, source TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO customers SELECT email, name, 'shop' FROM customers_a
INSERT OR IGNORE INTO customers SELECT email, name, 'support' FROM customers_b
SELECT email, name, source FROM customers ORDER BY email

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
email	name	source
ana@x.com	Ana Ruiz	shop
bo@x.com	Bo Lind	shop
cy@x.com	Cy Young	support

Three customers emerge from four input rows: Ana and Bo from the shop, Cy from support - and Bo's support row was the one overlap, set aside by INSERT OR IGNORE under the stated rule 'shop record wins', with the calculator confirming 2 + 2 - 1 overlap = 3. Three properties make this a migration rather than a shrug. First, the dedupe rule is explicit and chosen by the business before the merge (which source is authoritative for shared people, and what happens to fields where the loser had better data - here the support variant of Bo's name was discarded entirely, a decision someone should consciously make). Second, the source column preserves provenance, so a later 'why does Bo's record say that' has an answer. Third, nothing was silent: inputs 4, outputs 3, overlap 1 - if those numbers do not reconcile, the merge does not ship. What INSERT OR IGNORE must never become is a habit: it suppresses every constraint violation, not just the expected duplicates, so run it with a pre-merge duplicate report in hand and a post-merge reconciliation, or the day it swallows a genuinely corrupt row, nobody will know.
We need UNIQUE(email) on users, but the table has years of duplicate emails. The index creation fails. What's the correct order of operations?
Clean first, constrain second - and use the failure itself as the audit tool. The duplicate census, then the constraint:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ana@x.com'), (2, 'bo@x.com'), (3, 'ana@x.com'), (4, 'cy@x.com'), (5, 'bo@x.com')
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS copies FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING copies > 1 ORDER BY email
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_users_email ON users (email)

messages.content: The census names the problem precisely: ana@x.com twice, bo@x.com twice - and the unique index creation fails, as it must, because you cannot declare a rule the data already breaks and expect the engine to guess which copies are real. The order of operations is: (1) enumerate duplicates with the GROUP BY ... HAVING query, which becomes the cleanup worklist; (2) decide per duplicate group which row survives and where the loser's relationships go - orders, logins, and history pointing at a deleted duplicate must be repointed to the survivor first, exactly as in a customer merge; (3) delete or merge the losers; (4) only then create the index, which now succeeds and stands guard. Teams that reverse steps 2 and 4 discover the failure at deployment time; teams that skip step 2's repointing create orphaned history. There is also a cultural step: duplicates accumulated because inserts were never checked, so pair the new index with a look at which writer created the copies - otherwise the index converts silent duplication into loud insert failures for a legacy import nobody updated, usually at the least convenient hour. Constraints ratify a cleaned reality; they do not clean it.
A lookup table has 5000 rows and WHERE email = ? is doing full scans. Walk me through adding the index as a schema change - and how we verify it exists and is used by our key query pattern.
Index creation as a deliberate migration step, with the catalog as the verification:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE accounts (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL)
INSERT INTO accounts WITH RECURSIVE c(value) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT value + 1 FROM c WHERE value < 5000) SELECT value, 'user' || value || '@x.com' FROM c
CREATE INDEX ix_accounts_email ON accounts (email)
PRAGMA index_list(accounts)

messages.name: database_query
messages.content:
seq	name	unique	origin	partial
0	ix_accounts_email	0	c	0

arguments.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS found FROM accounts WHERE email = 'user4999@x.com'

messages.content: The index now exists - PRAGMA index_list shows ix_accounts_email registered on the table - and the point lookup returns its one row. Framed as migration discipline rather than a one-off command: the index gets a name that states its purpose (ix_accounts_email), it is created in the same migration system as every other schema change (so staging and production agree), and its cost is acknowledged in the change description - build time and lock behavior on the live table, plus write amplification forever after, since every insert now maintains two structures. On a 5000-row table the build is instant; on 500 million rows the same statement is a planned operation (online index builds where the engine offers them, off-peak windows where it does not). Verification is two-layered: the catalog proves the index exists; an EXPLAIN of the production query proves the planner uses it - indexes the planner ignores are pure cost. Finally, indexes are the one schema object you may add speculatively with a clear conscience and drop without data loss, which is why 'add the index, measure, keep or drop' is a legitimate experiment, unlike most schema changes.
How do we track which schema version a database is at, so deployments and support can tell at a glance? Show me the mechanism.
A schema_migrations table inside the database itself - the schema carries its own version history:

arguments.sql: CREATE TABLE schema_migrations (version INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, description TEXT NOT NULL, applied_on TEXT NOT NULL)
